title: See What I Need, Dream What I Want: A Navigation Foundation Model on a Self-Constructed Representation Space
summary: What visual representation should a navigation policy act on? Navigation policies built on vision foundation models largely leave representation design to the encoders' pretraining objectives. We present RepresentNav, a navigation foundation model built on a self-constructed representation space: a visual representation constructed by the policy's own objectives from vision foundation models. RepresentNav builds this space with Representation Residuals, a compact three-layer transformer that attends over features spanning the full depth of multiple complementary vision foundation models, so that the policy learns to see what it needs for navigation. In the same space it dreams what it wants: before every action a latent chain-of-thought predicts the representation of the scene a moment ahead. The dream is trained end-to-end with the policy as a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), with a next-representation prediction loss and a regularizer on its targets. RepresentNav sets a new state of the art on VLNVerse, VLN-CE R2R, EVT-Bench, and two point-goal benchmarks, and its gains carry over to a physical robot amid clutter and moving people. On VLNVerse fine-grained, RepresentNav achieves 83.80% success, outperforming the previous state of the art by 20.05 percentage points, and on EVT-Bench distracted tracking it reaches 85.5% with a single camera (+10.1). With the same encoders, the self-constructed space clearly outperforms concatenating their outputs and learns to weight their layers unevenly, and a dream in it cuts collisions by a quarter. A single dreamed latent decodes into the depth, semantics, and 3D occupancy of the scene a moment ahead, more accurately than pretrained encoders applied to the real future frame, although occupancy is never supervised, and the rollout tracks the robot's own motion over the next second: the dream emerges as a compact latent world model.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Consider a robot asked to cross a cluttered hall to a point on its far side. What it needs to see is not every pixel but a representation: a description of the world that makes explicit what the next decision needs and leaves out the rest bengio2013representation . A person may name three things, how far the nearest surfaces are, what the objects around it are, and how those objects and the robot itself are moving; but what a representation should make explicit is a long-standing question in vision. One tradition answered that a general-purpose description of the scene should come first, built once for any task to read marr1982vision . The other answered that perception is purposive: it exists for action and should pick out only what the behavior at hand needs gibson1979ecological . Deep learning gave the second answer its mechanism: the task's own error, back-propagated into the representation lecun2015deep . Vision foundation models have since made the general-purpose tradition practical; navigation, building on them, has largely set the purposive one aside. A vision foundation model is a general-purpose description at a scale no one could have built by hand, but it makes explicit what its own objective needs and by its final layer has left out the rest, including much of the spatial structure it built along the way yosinski2014transferable,papyan2020prevalence,raghu2021vision ; most navigation policies built on vision-language models take that output through an interface fixed before the task exists zhang2025navfom,zhang2024uninavid,internvla2025 . Fine-tuning the encoder is only a partial remedy: it adapts one network behind the same output and can erode the general description kumar2022finetuning . They follow open-ended instructions and track a person described in words, yet still misjudge free space, collide with obstacles they could describe, and lose a target that turns a corner. The field has more general-purpose visual prior than ever, yet its policies have little say over what they see. We argue that the two answers need no longer exclude each other in embodied navigation. With vision foundation models a general-purpose description now exists, so the purposive step can be taken on top of it rather than instead of it, and the action gradient is the instrument for taking it. We call the result a self-constructed representation space: a representation constructed by the policy's own objectives out of the internal structure of vision foundation models. We present (RepNav), a navigation foundation model that sees and dreams in such a space. It builds the space with (Fig.~ fig:representnav_overview a), a compact three-layer transformer that attends over layers spanning the full depth of three complementary vision foundation models, semantic, geometric, and dynamic; what it makes explicit is found in training and differs across regions of one view. title: SEVI: Safe Evidential Real-World Reinforcement Learning
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures. Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L), 2026. Project page: https://sevi-safe.github.io/
summary: Real-world reinforcement learning has enabled contact-rich manipulation tasks to be trained directly on physical robots, but unsafe interactions during online learning remain a key barrier to practical deployment. We propose Safe Evidential Real-World Reinforcement Learning (SEVI), a framework for reliability-aware safety intervention during real-world policy learning. SEVI introduces an Evidential Safety Critic that estimates both future constraint-violation risk and epistemic uncertainty in a single forward pass. During online learning, SEVI evaluates each task-policy action before execution; if the action is predicted to be unsafe or the prediction is insufficiently supported by evidence, SEVI overrides it with an offline-trained recovery policy that guides the robot toward a lower-risk region. We evaluate SEVI on two simulated manipulation tasks and a real-world USB insertion task under in-distribution and distribution-shifted conditions. Across task-learning and safety-critic baselines, SEVI achieves the strongest trajectory-level safety prediction, the highest final task success, and the lowest unsafe-event counts. SEVI also reduces unsafe events by 13.4 to 57.1 percent relative to recovery-based safe RL while preserving low-latency execution-time filtering. The project page is available at: https://sevi-safe.github.io/

The project page is available at: https://sevi-safe.github.io/ . Safe RL, Manipulation, Safety, Uncertainty. Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of enabling robots to acquire complex manipulation skills through trial and error. Recent real-world RL systems have shown that contact-rich manipulation tasks can be trained directly on hardware within a practical time budget. These systems typically rely on demonstrations, sample-efficient off-policy learning, learned rewards, and carefully designed controllers ball2023efficientonlinereinforcementlearning,luo2024serl . However, training RL on physical robots remains challenging because exploration can lead to unsafe interactions, such as excessive contact forces, object damage, workspace violations, or failures requiring human intervention. Therefore, as real-world RL becomes increasingly sample-efficient, a central remaining challenge is to reduce unsafe interactions during online training. This challenge is particularly pronounced in complex tasks, where safety depends on perception, object geometry, contact dynamics, and the evolving task policy zhu2020ingredientsrealworldroboticreinforcement . Existing real-world RL pipelines provide an effective foundation for online learning with prior data and off-policy updates. However, they do not explicitly address the autonomous intervention problem: determining when a proposed task action should be rejected and replaced by safe recovery behavior. One way to address this intervention problem is to augment the task policy with a recovery mechanism. Recovery-based safe RL methods instantiate this idea by switching to a recovery policy when a learned safety critic predicts future constraint violations thananjeyan2021recovery . A key limitation is that these intervention decisions rely on the reliability of the learned safety estimate, which may degrade under partial observations or in state-action regions poorly represented in prior data. Existing approaches to uncertainty-aware safety attempt to detect unreliable predictions under distribution shift seo2025uncertainty . World-model-based safety filters use learned latent dynamics to imagine future outcomes and identify potential out-of-distribution (OOD) failures Nakamura_2025 . Although this is a promising direction, it relies on accurate long-horizon prediction and sufficient coverage of safety-critical interactions. In complex manipulation, limited unsafe data and partial observability can cause learned dynamics to produce optimistic predictions in unfamiliar regions, leading unsafe actions to be classified as safe. Although sampling-based uncertainty methods can improve reliability estimation, ensembles lakshminarayanan2017simplescalablepredictiveuncertainty and Monte Carlo dropout gal2016dropoutbayesianapproximationrepresenting require multiple models or repeated forward passes, which increases latency for real-time robot control amini2020deep . To address this problem, we propose Safe Evidential Real-World Reinforcement Learning (SEVI), a framework for uncertainty-aware autonomous intervention during online real-world RL. SEVI introduces an Evidential Safety Critic (ESC), which models safety prediction as evidence accumulation and estimates both future constraint-violation risk and epistemic uncertainty in a single forward pass. Unlike sampling-based uncertainty methods, the ESC does not require ensembles or repeated stochastic inference, making it suitable for low-latency safety decisions. During online training, SEVI evaluates each action proposed by the task policy using both predicted risk and prediction reliability. If the action is predicted to be unsafe or the prediction is insufficiently supported by evidence, SEVI overrides the task action with an offline-trained recovery policy that guides the robot toward a lower-risk region as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser . This intervention mechanism reduces unsafe interactions without modifying the underlying off-policy RL objective. We evaluate SEVI on two simulated manipulation tasks and a real-world USB insertion task with a Franka robot. The experiments show that SEVI improves safety prediction under distribution shift, provides better-calibrated uncertainty than dropout and ensemble baselines, and reduces unsafe events during online real-world RL while maintaining strong task performance. In summary, this paper makes the following contributions: We introduce a modular real-world RL safety architecture that decouples task-policy learning from execution-time safety intervention while preserving the underlying task-learning objective. We propose an Evidential Safety Critic that estimates both future constraint-violation risk and epistemic uncertainty in a single forward pass, enabling low-latency reliability-aware safety assessment. We integrate evidential safety prediction with an offline-trained recovery policy to enable autonomous intervention during online real-world RL with prior data, while remaining compatible with standard off-policy RL pipelines. Related Work Real-world RL. Efficient learning from limited physical interaction remains challenging in the presence of high-dimensional observations, sparse rewards, and practical reset constraints. Recent progress has combined demonstrations or prior data with sample-efficient off-policy RL, enabling policies to be trained directly on physical robots within practical time budgets ball2023efficientonlinereinforcementlearning . Sample Efficient Robotic Reinforcement Learning (SERL) provides a full-stack real-world RL pipeline that integrates robot control, reward inference, asynchronous training, and Reinforcement Learning with Prior Data (RLPD) off-policy updates for manipulation tasks luo2024serl . These systems demonstrate that real-world RL can be practical when algorithmic and system-level components are carefully integrated. For complex manipulation tasks, online training can still require long hardware sessions with continuous human monitoring, resets, or corrective intervention. This supervision burden limits scalability, especially when unsafe behavior can occur during exploration. SEVI targets this bottleneck by adding an autonomous safety layer that rejects risky or unreliable task actions and invokes recovery during online training. Safe RL. Classical safe RL commonly formulates safety through constrained policy optimization~ achiam2017constrained , while control-theoretic approaches use control barrier functions or Hamilton--Jacobi reachability to enforce safety~ ames2019control,chen2023hamilton . Predictive and latent safety filters extend safety reasoning to learned models and high-dimensional observations~ Nakamura_2025 . Such approaches often rely on predefined constraints, dynamics models, or explicit safety specifications. Recovery-based methods are more closely related to SEVI, as they override risky task actions before unsafe states are reached~ thananjeyan2021recovery . However, these methods typically trigger intervention from predicted risk alone, which may become unreliable under partial observations, policy-induced distribution shift, or limited data coverage. SEVI additionally considers the reliability of the safety estimate when determining whether recovery is required. Uncertainty and Failure Prediction. Uncertainty estimation is widely used to identify unreliable predictions in learned robotic systems. Monte Carlo dropout and deep ensembles estimate epistemic uncertainty through stochastic inference or model disagreement~ gal2016dropoutbayesianapproximationrepresenting,lakshminarayanan2017simplescalablepredictiveuncertainty . These methods are effective, but they require repeated forward passes or multiple models, which increases latency for real-time robot control. Recent failure-detection methods monitor deviations from successful behavior. For example, FAIL-Detect formulates runtime failure detection as sequential OOD detection and uses conformal prediction to detect failures from successful rollouts alone~ xu2025can . Such methods improve runtime awareness, but they mainly serve as monitors and do not directly provide autonomous intervention for online RL. Evidential learning provides a sampling-free alternative for uncertainty estimation. Instead of sampling over network weights or model instances, it models prediction as evidence accumulation and estimates uncertainty from the parameters of an evidential distribution~ amini2020deep . Building on this formulation, our Evidential Safety Critic predicts both future violation risk and epistemic uncertainty in a single forward pass. This design connects uncertainty estimation to action selection: recovery is triggered when an action is either high-risk or insufficiently supported by evidence. title: FORCA: A Force-Aware Coding Agent for Contact-Rich Robot Manipulation
summary: Coding agents can translate language instructions into robot programs. For contact-rich manipulation, a key challenge is to generate and refine control logic that responds to physical interaction. We present FORCA, a coding agent that takes visual observations and wrist force/torque (F/T) measurements as input to write Python programs for contact probing and force-responsive motion. Between executions, the agent inspects force records alongside visual outcomes to diagnose failures and revise both motion and force-feedback control logic. FORCA requires no demonstrations, task-specific training, or simulation. Across five real-robot tasks, we demonstrate its effectiveness in three forms of contact-rich manipulation: improving manipulation accuracy, adapting to changes in object or surface properties, and regulating contact under surface variation and object motion. Compared with a vision-only variant of the same agent, FORCA improves grasp accuracy and task success and reduces contact loss in wiping and peeling.

Introduction sec:intro Coding agents based on foundation models turn open-ended instructions into executable robot programs that compose perception, grasping, and motion skills liang2023codeaspolicies,singh2023progprompt,huang2023voxposer,huang2024rekep . They ground their decisions mainly in vision and proprioception, which is often insufficient for contact-rich manipulation: occluded or reflective surfaces yield uncertain geometry, mass and friction are not visible, and maintaining contact requires responding to surface variation and object motion. Force and contact measurements complement vision by providing evidence about contact states and mechanical responses that are difficult to infer from visual observations alone. Learned policies exploit force and tactile signals for reactive control but require demonstrations or robot data foar2024,forcevla2025,tla2025,tactilevla2025 . Foundation-model agents have used force through compliant or force-thresholded primitives genchip2024,ellmer2025 , inferred physical properties largely from priors deligrasp2024,llmphy2024,coral2026 , and revised force targets after failed attempts xie2025unfettered . Supporting these diverse tasks requires agents to determine when contact information is needed, how it should guide ongoing motion, and how unexpected contact outcomes should inform subsequent attempts. We present , a training-free coding agent that uses wrist force/torque (F/T) sensing in both program execution and program revision (Fig.~ fig:method:overview ). It writes complete Python programs with access to the measured wrench. During a rollout, the program uses measurements from contact probes to guide subsequent actions and uses live force feedback to regulate its motion. Between rollouts, the agent relates the recorded force traces to visual outcomes, diagnoses failures, and revises the program. addresses three types of contact-rich manipulation: (i)~precision manipulation, where force cues help refine grasp poses and improve manipulation accuracy; (ii)~physical adaptation, where actions must be adjusted to changes in object or surface properties; and (iii)~contact regulation, where motion must respond to surface variation and object movement. We evaluate on five real-robot tasks spanning these categories: drawer opening, door-handle operation, cube-to-target knocking, vase wiping, and cucumber peeling. Compared with a vision-only variant of the same agent, increases task success from 40 to 100 for drawer opening and from 10 to 100 for door-handle operation, while reducing contact-loss rates in wiping and peeling from 40.6--55.9 to at most 2.2 . Our contributions are twofold. First, we introduce a coding-agent framework that generates task-specific motion and force-feedback control logic from language instructions. The resulting programs use measured contact to refine grasp poses and regulate motion during execution. Second, we extend program refinement to the force-feedback logic itself, enabling coding agents to revise how their programs respond to contact based on evidence from real-robot execution. Method sec:method Given a language instruction and RGB-D observations, writes a Python code with access to wrist force/torque (F/T) measurements. The program executes on the robot without querying the foundation model. After execution, the agent reviews the recorded interaction and revises the code (Fig.~ fig:method:overview ). We refer to one execution of a program as a rollout. Force-Aware Program Synthesis sec:method:synthesis For each task, the agent generates a Python task program that specifies the action sequence and the force-dependent motion logic. To construct this program, the agent has access to an initial skill codebase for perception, grasping, motion planning, and pick-and-place, assembled from open-source components under human supervision. These predefined modules provide object pose estimates, grasp candidates, and collision-free trajectories computed with PyRoKi~ pyroki2025 . Figure~ fig:method:skills illustrates these modules as the robot acquires a whiteboard eraser for the instruction ``Wipe the vase.'' The agent writes the force-dependent logic for each task using wrist wrench measurements exposed by the robot interface. For example, this logic can specify when an approach should stop or how motion should respond to a force error. title: EgoForesight: Effectively Scaling Policy Learning with Noisy Egocentric Actions
summary: Scaling policy learning requires broad experience and reliable supervision. Robot demonstrations provide high-quality trajectory supervision but are costly to collect. Egocentric videos broaden task and environment coverage, yet motion reconstruction and retargeting introduce noisy action labels. To address this challenge, we introduce EgoForesight, a vision-language-action framework that learns jointly from both sources by reducing the influence of unreliable action labels and exploiting demonstrated outcomes as complementary supervision. A joint vision-action flow couples future visual representation prediction with action generation, unifying reliability-aware action learning with outcome-informed representation transfer. Specifically, reliability-conditioned corruption allocates action supervision across noise levels according to source reliability, while reliability-weighted regression regulates each source's contribution. Complementing this treatment of noisy labels, privileged-future representation distillation draws supervision from demonstrated outcomes. An exponential-moving-average teacher observes the current scene and clean future to encode action-relevant structure from the resulting scene change. Its deeper representations supervise an earlier student layer receiving a corrupted future, providing outcome-informed structure beyond noisy action annotations. Together, these mechanisms support effective scaling with noisy egocentric actions. Over the tested range, EgoForesight exhibits steeper scaling slopes than the baseline, reducing real-world open-loop action MSE by 20.5% and improving RoboCasa few-shot success by 8.1 percentage points at 30,000 hours of pretraining data. After post-training, it also achieves strong absolute performance in both simulated and real-world dexterous manipulation.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect broad visual and linguistic knowledge to robot control~ brohan2023rt2,black2024pi0 . We organize their supervision into an embodied data pyramid: vision--language data offer semantic coverage, egocentric demonstrations capture diverse interactions, and robot trajectories provide executable controls but require dedicated hardware and collection effort~ hoque2025egodex,oxe2023,khazatsky2024droid . EgoMimic~ kareer2024egomimic and EgoScale~ zheng2026egoscale demonstrate the value of egocentric data through human--robot co-training and large-scale policy pretraining. However, recovering actions from egocentric videos introduces annotation noise. Camera tracking and hand-pose reconstruction can produce errors, particularly under occlusion and rapid motion~ zhang2025hawor,hoque2025egodex . Retargeting adds a geometric mismatch: differences in palm size, finger proportions, and joint structure mean that accurately tracked human poses need not admit an equivalent robot configuration~ wang2024dexcap,xin2026retargeting . Appearance and dynamics further complicate transfer. Effective learning from egocentric data therefore requires more than increasing its scale: policies must limit the influence of unreliable action labels while drawing on supervision beyond those labels, enabling additional ego-data to provide effective supervision. To meet these requirements, we introduce , a VLA framework that reduces the influence of unreliable actions while learning from demonstrated outcomes. Inspired by prior unified video--action and dynamics--action models~ zhu2025uwm,lyu2026lda , our design couples experts for future visual representations and action chunks and trains them with modality-specific flow-matching paths. Separate corruption times control the information available in the vision and action streams, allowing us to regulate noisy action supervision and distill outcome-informed representations within the same model. First, reliability-conditioned corruption allocates action supervision across noise levels according to source reliability. Motivated by ADP's finding that stronger diffusion noise can contract target and suboptimal distributions~ wei2026ambientpolicy , our continuous source-reliability schedule shifts less reliable actions toward stronger corruption. Reliability-weighted action regression complements this schedule by controlling how strongly each source contributes to learning. Together, they enable learning from diverse egocentric data without assuming uniformly reliable labels. Second, privileged-future representation distillation draws on demonstrated outcomes for action-relevant evidence beyond noisy annotations. An exponential-moving-average (EMA) teacher receives the current observation and observed future at the clean endpoint, acting as a conditional inverse dynamics model (IDM). Initialized from higher-quality demonstrations, the teacher provides action representations informed by the observed scene change. Adapting Self-Flow's cleaner, noise-shifted EMA teacher and cross-layer alignment~ chefer2026selfflow , we apply this mechanism to robot action tokens: a deeper teacher feature supervises an earlier student layer, which enriches early policy features with outcome-informed structure. In our setting, observed-future conditioning gives the teacher its inverse-dynamics role, and the student learns to anticipate the resulting outcome-informed representation while receiving a corrupted future. For model training, we first establish visual--action correspondences on higher-quality robot demonstrations and curated egocentric trajectories. This checkpoint initializes the student and teacher before training expands to a larger action-annotated egocentric-data mixture with reliability-conditioned corruption and privileged-future distillation enabled. Our experiments examine scaling as a test of how effectively policies use noisy egocentric supervision. Under matched data and optimization budgets, \ translates added pretraining data into stronger gains in action prediction and closed-loop control. Ablations support complementary roles for reliability conditioning and future distillation, and show the value of establishing action correspondences on higher-quality data before expanding coverage. title: Full-Weight VLA Fine-Tuning Without an fp32 Master Copy Silently Erases Most Updates
summary: When a vision-language-action (VLA) model is fine-tuned with its trainable weights in bfloat16 (bf16) and no fp32 master copy, AdamW writes each update straight into bf16, silently rounding away any update smaller than 1/512 of a weight. In 9 of 12 open VLA codebases a default or documented recipe trains this way, 4 on full weight matrices, including LeRobot's SmolVLA default and its $π_0$/$π_{0.5}$ guides. In our LIBERO runs without the copy, a probe every 100 steps finds at least 79% of updates to bf16 weights erased. On the Hugging Face Hub, 99% of sampled full-weight SmolVLA fine-tunes store the action expert in bf16, and 84% of recent $π_{0.5}$ fine-tunes with a training configuration set the bf16 flag. On LIBERO-Object, with rules fixed in advance, an fp32 copy raises success over LeRobot's storage from 4.3% to 49.3% for SmolVLA and from 5.1% to 80.9% for $π_{0.5}$ at a ten-times lower learning rate, where both models are undertrained, and from 89.0% to 97.7% for $π_{0.5}$ at its default rate. For SmolVLA at its default rate it adds 10.2 points with open-loop 50-action chunks but only 4.2 when re-planning every 10 actions. In these five comparisons and two more against SmolVLA with every trainable weight in bf16, every run with the copy beats every run without it (p < 0.05); all gaps but the 8.7- and 4.2-point ones clear our 10-point threshold. The fix is to keep the trainable weights in fp32 during training, a one-line change for SmolVLA in LeRobot.

title: Distributed Swarm Morphogenesis with Neural Cellular Automata
summary: Swarm morphogenesis requires robots to assemble desired shapes through local interactions. We present a modular framework integrating neural cellular automata (NCA) with existing site selection and collision-aware control. Within this framework, we introduce a decentralized attachment-site discovery mechanism. Robots already in the formation update and share local NCA states to identify new attachment sites, enabling progressive growth without a predefined list of sites during deployment. To bridge the mismatch between conventional NCA growth and gradual physical assembly, we additionally propose offline sparse-retention fine-tuning that simulates partial attachment, together with a false-positive loss that penalizes invalid site activations. Simulations demonstrate formation of diverse lattice morphologies, scaling to several hundred robots, and substantial improvements in morphology accuracy from the proposed fine-tuning. Experiments with Crazyflie quadrotors validate the integrated execution pipeline using robot-relative observations reconstructed from external tracking.

Introduction sec:introduction Swarm morphogenesis aims to generate large-scale physical structures through local interactions among robots. Applications include coordinated aerial displays, distributed inspection, search, surveillance, and defence, where formations may need to scale or adapt across environments. Reliance on GPS, motion capture, or centralized estimation can limit applicability where signals or infrastructure are unavailable, including GNSS-denied environments; relative-sensing approaches instead use onboard vision~ montijano2016vision , ranging and odometry~ guo2020uwb , or distance-only measurements~ suttner2018distance,lu2025concurrent . Here, we consider local-relative sensing without globally referenced robot poses. Distributed task-allocation methods assign tasks to robots~ choi2009consensus , while assignment-based shape-formation methods allocate or dynamically select robot goals~ wang2020taskswapping,li2025distributed . Assignment-free methods guide robots to fill specified shapes without explicit robot-to-site assignments~ sun2023meanshift,zhang2024meanshift . These approaches differ in how robots occupy the shape, but both assume its geometry is supplied beforehand. We instead consider distributed attachment-site discovery.Essentially, we determine which physical attachment sites should exist as the morphology develops, so that a global structure can emerge from a local developmental rule trained offline, rather than a stored goal list. Existing assignment and control methods then coordinate robots to occupy these sites. NCAs suit distributed attachment-site discovery because local computations generate global structure without a central coordinator. Each cell updates its state from neighbors, enabling pattern growth and regeneration~ mordvintsev2020growing , with extensions to graphs and higher-resolution generation~ grattarola2021learning,gala2024equivariant,pajouheshgar2026cells . We use these states to discover physical attachment sites, establishing a first step toward neural swarm morphogenesis. The framework separates NCA attachment-site generation from assignment and control, allowing independent replacement. These methods can be replaced without altering NCA attachment-site generation. We use the artificial-light-field assignment and constrained controller of~ li2025distributed . Standard Growing NCAs train on virtual grids without assembly constraints. We propose an NCA-based framework for distributed swarm morphogenesis with three main contributions: Modular lattice-morphogenesis framework. We couple developmental attachment-site generation, distributed assignment, and collision-aware control. Distributed attachment-site discovery method. Robots in the formation exchange and update local NCA states to identify candidate attachment sites to occupy. This allows the formation to develop progressively without providing robots with a complete list of attachment sites. Offline fine-tuning adapts a pretrained NCA to physical assembly using simulated partial attachment. An additional false-positive loss penalizes activation outside the desired morphology. Background and Related Work sec:background Three aspects frame swarm morphogenesis: a) spatial representation and localization, b) robot coordination and assembly, and c) local developmental mechanisms. They address how desired structures are represented and sensed, occupied by robots, and generated through local rules. Formation-control methods vary in geometric representation and spatial-information requirements~ oh2015survey . GPS or indoor positioning systems have been used in~ yang2019indoor ; relative approaches use vision, ranging, odometry, or distance measurements~ montijano2016vision,guo2020uwb,suttner2018distance,lu2025concurrent . Shapes can be represented as continuous regions or density fields~ xiang2026density , or discrete lattices~ nie2023triangular . We adopt lattices for their well-defined attachment sites during progressive assembly. Distributed task allocation provides coordination mechanisms~ choi2009consensus . Shape-formation methods use task swapping or dynamic assignment~ wang2020taskswapping,li2025distributed , assignment-free strategies~ sun2023meanshift,zhang2024meanshift , or learned decentralized control~ jiang2023gnn . Progressive self-assembly methods incorporate robots incrementally into a developing formation~ rubenstein2014programmable,li2019progressive,pan2024crystallization . Although these approaches differ in how robots join or occupy a shape, they rely on prescribed geometry or designed assembly rules rather than learned local attachment-site generation. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) enable learned decentralized interactions through neighborhood message passing~ jiang2023gnn . Our NCA follows a similar principle but operates on a regular lattice rather than a general graph. Its shared symbolic frame preserves neighbor directions, allowing spatially ordered updates without permutation-invariant aggregation or explicit edge features. We therefore formulate progressive attachment-site generation using the simpler NCA setting, without requiring the general GNN framework. Morphogenetic approaches generate structure through local rules, including gene-regulatory models~ meng2013morphogenetic and reaction--diffusion dynamics demonstrated in robot swarms~ slavkov2018morphogenesis . NCAs use learned local updates to generate and regenerate patterns~ mordvintsev2020growing , with extensions to graph-based interactions~ grattarola2021learning,gala2024equivariant . Consequently, these methods provide no directly comparable baseline for learned local attachment-site generation under incremental physical assembly. title: DiscoDemo: Discovering Efficient and Diverse Robot Demonstrations for Imitation Learning
summary: Behavior cloning for robotic manipulation is highly sensitive to the coverage of its training data, yet collecting diverse successful demonstrations remains costly. We study reinforcement learning (RL) not as a deployable controller, but as a data generator for downstream visuomotor imitation learning. Our key premise is that multiple successful solution modes cover a broader range of successful trajectories than repeatedly collecting a single narrow solution. We introduce DiscoDemo, which trains a privileged latent-conditioned RL generator with a parallel reverse curriculum and a success-gated diversity objective to discover diverse solutions while preserving task success. The trained generator produces multiple successful closed-loop behaviors, which are safety-filtered and exported as a static dataset for downstream imitation learning. Across four manipulation tasks, DiscoDemo produces broader successful-state coverage and improves downstream visuomotor policies in both simulation and the real world. Averaged across tasks, downstream success increases to 62% from 40% for the strongest baseline in simulation, and to 78% from 39% on the real robot, respectively. These results suggest that successful solution diversity improves imitation learning for a pretrained flow-matching VLA and remains complementary to corrective data collection. Scaling this paradigm, however, is constrained by the cost of physical data collection. Robot trajectories are typically collected through human teleoperation, requiring access to physical robot hardware and operator time for every episode. Consequently, even large robot datasets contain only on the order of a million episodes~ o2024open,khazatsky2024droid , far fewer than the billions of image--text pairs~ schuhmann2022laion or trillions of tokens~ llama3 used to train foundation models in vision and language. Simulation offers a scalable alternative. Robot trajectories can be generated cheaply and in parallel without requiring human teleoperation for every episode, and advances in sim-to-real transfer have made simulated experience increasingly useful for training real-world policies~ torne2024reconciling,bauza2024demostart . Scaling simulated data, however, raises two key questions: how should successful trajectories be generated, and what distribution of successful behavior should they cover? Together, these choices determine the supervision available to downstream BC. Existing simulation pipelines generate successful trajectories in several ways. Motion-planning methods construct feasible motions between task-relevant poses~ chen2025robotwin,chen2025internvla,tian2026interndata , but rely on task-specific planning structure. MimicGen-style methods reduce this burden by retargeting successful demonstration segments to new scene configurations~ mimicgen,skillmimicgen,jiang2025dexmimicgen , but remain constrained by the behaviors contained in the source demonstrations and by where those behaviors can be successfully retargeted. These limitations are particularly relevant in contact-rich manipulation, where geometric transformation alone may not preserve successful interactions as the scene changes. Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a complementary approach by learning closed-loop behavior directly from task feedback, and recent methods bootstrap RL from demonstrations or pretrained behavior priors to make successful data generation practical under sparse rewards~ rfcl,pld,xu2026expertgen . However, an RL policy that reliably solves the task does not necessarily generate a training distribution well suited to downstream BC. As illustrated in , task reward alone can concentrate an RL policy around a narrow set of successful solutions, so collecting more rollouts need not substantially expand the states represented in the dataset~ smerl . This limited coverage can make BC brittle when prediction errors move the learned policy beyond states supported by its training demonstrations~ dagger . Perturbation- and recovery-based methods broaden supervision around an existing demonstration or policy~ dai2026pgdg,pld , but their additional experience remains anchored to the supplied behavior. This motivates a different question: can the generator itself discover multiple successful ways of solving the task? We address this question with , which trains an RL generator to combine task competence with solution diversity. Starting from a few successful demonstrations, we use a parallel reverse curriculum to bootstrap task-solving behavior under sparse rewards, using demonstration states for curriculum resets rather than treating demonstration actions as the target solution. At the same time, we condition the generator on a latent skill and optimize a success-gated diversity objective that encourages different skills to realize distinct state-space behaviors while preserving task completion~ smerl,park2024metra . The resulting generator discovers multiple successful solution modes whose union provides broader successful-state coverage for downstream BC. We evaluate on four real-world manipulation tasks reconstructed in simulation, spanning pick-and-place, stacking, and precision-sensitive peg insertion. These approaches broaden scene, state, and recovery coverage from existing demonstrations or behaviors. Our work similarly studies the distribution produced by an RL generator, but discovers diverse successful solutions online with a latent-conditioned, success-gated objective. summary: Long-horizon robot tasks require retaining and using past information. We integrate Test-Time Training (TTT), which stores context in fast weights, into InternVLA-A1 and Pi0.5 to study action generation conditioned on human demonstrations through training on paired demonstrations and robot trajectories. We implement memory transfer between the two phases and truncated backpropagation, and examine training objectives, gradient coverage, and contrastive regularization across video, short-video, and single-frame cue tasks. In our experiments, adding TTT and training on paired data at the current scale did not lead to consistent target selection based on demonstrations. Under the tested settings, shorter sequences, full trajectory gradient connectivity, and contrastive regularization did not clearly improve responsiveness to demonstrations. When demonstrations were reduced to single-frame cues, real-robot execution still showed a preference for cups at fixed positions. We document the implementation, training configurations, and observations to support further inspection and replication.

Introduction Our overall goal is to explore the memory capabilities needed for long-horizon robot tasks. Later decisions may depend on information encountered much earlier, so models need to retain and use historical context. We therefore consider Test-Time Training (TTT) 1 . TTT writes past information into a fixed-size memory state by updating fast weights. Unlike caches that grow with history length, its memory-state storage remains constant during inference, offering a substantial advantage for long-horizon tasks. TTT also supports online updates and end-to-end learning of memory writes and reads. These properties motivate our exploration. We focus on robot action generation conditioned on human demonstrations. Each training sample pairs a human demonstration with its corresponding robot trajectory. The model first reads the demonstration, then processes the robot trajectory using the resulting memory. TTT provides the memory mechanism, while task training teaches the model how demonstration conditions should affect action generation. We implement a standard TTT layer and integrate it into Pi0.5 2 and InternVLA-A1 3 . Following the TBPTT approach in RoboTTT 4 , we organize state transfer and gradient propagation between human demonstrations and robot trajectories. Our main contribution is to reproduce and clearly describe the TTT architecture and its training procedure for combining human demonstrations with robot trajectories in VLA models. Training infrastructure constraints have limited the scale of pretraining and training on memory-task data, leaving TTT's memory capabilities insufficiently trained and evaluated. We also report observations across task settings and discuss training objectives, evaluation protocols, and contrastive regularization. We leave unresolved causes and incomplete validation explicitly open. Related Work From Test-Time Adaptation to Parametric Memory sec:2.1 Early Test-Time Training (TTT) 5 primarily addressed distribution shifts between training and test data. The model constructs a self-supervised task from unlabeled test inputs and updates its parameters before prediction. TTT++ 6 and TTT-MAE 7 later explored adaptation through feature-distribution alignment and masked image reconstruction, respectively. Subsequent work incorporated inner learning into the model architecture. MTTT 8 learns the inner self-supervised task through outer-loop task training. TTT layers 1 use the inner model's weights as recurrent state, continually compressing historical context into those weights. Titans 9 and TTT-E2E 10 also explore retaining context through test-time parameter updates, treating these updates as memory writes. In the TTT layer 1 used here, the model constructs \(K\), \(V\), and \(Q\) from the input. The inner model writes information into fast weights by learning to predict \(V\) from \(K\), then reads it using \(Q\). Outer-loop task training learns how this information should be written and used. The inner model, objective, and update rule jointly define the design space. TTT across Domains sec:2.2 In language modeling, TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP 1 store historical state in a linear model and a two-layer MLP, respectively. Titans 9 combines long-term neural memory with local attention. TTT-E2E 10 updates weights through next-token prediction and learns their initialization through meta-training. These methods all absorb context through parameter updates, but differ in their memory structures and inner objectives. In vision, TTT-MAE 7 uses masked reconstruction for test-time adaptation, while MTTT 8 uses inner learning as a visual representation module. ViT³ 11 further examines inner models, losses, and update rules, including full-batch updates, inner learning rates, model capacity, and convolutional structures. These choices inform the implementation of visual TTT. For video, TTT on Video Streams 12 carries forward previously updated parameters and adapts online to incoming frames. One-Minute Video Generation 13 retains local attention in a pretrained video model and uses TTT to transfer context across segments. These methods illustrate different ways to process temporal information, but their training procedures still require adaptation to robot tasks. TTT for Robot Policies sec:2.3 RoboTTT 4 introduces fast-weight memory into an action model and combines Sequence Action Forcing with TBPTT for sequence training. Human videos update memory without providing action supervision; subsequent robot trajectories inherit that memory and contribute action losses. WAM-TTT 14 instead adds TTT to the video branch, updating memory through video prediction and key–value reconstruction and learning its connection to actions through task losses on paired robot data. Recent work further explores how memory is organized. RecastVLA 15 updates shared fast weights using action-generation features. T²Mem 16 forms memory from observations and learns to retain and use it through action supervision. TTT-RM 17 uses historical reconstruction residuals so that fast weights can supplement information missing from current observations and explicit memory. These studies examine memory interfaces, update timing, and learning objectives. Drawing on these memory mechanisms and training approaches, we integrate TTT into Pi0.5 2 and InternVLA-A1 3 and explore training with human demonstrations and robot trajectories. We focus on how demonstration information enters fast weights and how robot supervision constrains its use. The following sections describe the implementation and experimental observations. We first outline sequence training in RoboTTT, then describe the connection between human demonstrations and robot trajectories and the independent configuration of their memory-write frequencies. They are updated during outer-loop task training and remain fixed during inference. The added TTT layer contains both slow and fast weights. title: Coupling Execution Horizon and Sampling Depth in Flow-Matching VLA Policies
summary: Flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate expressive continuous trajectories for robotic manipulation, yet balancing real-time responsiveness with execution stability remains a persistent challenge. Standard deployment workflows typically treat numerical solver depth and execution horizon as decoupled choices. The horizon amortizes inference latency, while solver depth is kept high to preserve integration fidelity. In this paper, we reveal a fundamental compute-execution coupling in flow-matching VLAs governed by a systematic sign reversal. While coarse numerical integration degrades precision under rapid replanning, it markedly improves task performance under extended open-loop commitment. Geometrically, numerical truncation contracts lateral action dispersion around an invariant trajectory centroid, serving as an implicit regularizer that suppresses compounding open-loop drift. Across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world Franka manipulation on representative VLA backbones including $π_0$, $π_{0.5}$, and GR00T, exploiting this joint coupling consistently achieves superior task success while drastically lowering inference latency, entirely training-free and without architectural modifications. These findings establish numerical sampling depth as an operational variance regulator, shifting its role from a static precision budget to an active deployment knob in robot learning. Deployment typically fixes two operational parameters, namely the execution horizon , the open-loop action prefix executed before re-querying the policy, and the sampling depth , the numerical integration steps allocated per chunk (equaling the number of function evaluations under forward Euler). For example, standard benchmark protocols for on LIBERO conventionally default to . Prevailing deployment practices treat and as independent choices. Receding-horizon frameworks~ black2025rtc,liu2024bid sweep execution horizons to amortize perception latency while holding solver depth fixed. Conversely, policy acceleration methods~ prasad2024consistency,wang2024onedp,luan2026snapflow distill or truncate numerical ODE solvers primarily under standard, short horizons. title: PPO vs. SAC: A Comparative Study for Cooperative Motion Control of Dual-Arm Space Robots
comment: Presented at the 2026 AAS/AIAA Astrodynamics Specialist Conference, Whistler, British Columbia, Canada, July 26-30, 2026. Paper AAS 26-740
summary: The growing population of orbital debris has intensified interest in active debris removal and on-orbit servicing, for which dual-arm space manipulators offer improved grasping stability and load distribution relative to single-arm systems. However, coordinating two manipulators under inter-arm collision avoidance, orientation alignment, and sensing uncertainty remains challenging. This paper develops a coordinated reinforcement learning framework for cooperative motion planning of a dual-arm space manipulator in a target-reaching task with inter-arm collision-avoidance constraints. A centralized state representation combines joint-space, end-effector, and target-relative information, while a multi-objective reward function promotes target-reaching accuracy, orientation alignment, motion smoothness, synchronized task completion, and collision avoidance. Within this framework, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) are compared as representative on-policy and off-policy algorithms, and the learned policies are further evaluated for generalization to previously unseen target configurations. Across five random seeds, SAC substantially outperforms PPO within the considered fixed-base simulation scenarios: it reaches an 80% success threshold in every seed (median 1.6M environment steps) whereas PPO does not reach it within a 4M-step budget, and it attains a higher mean success rate (78.6% versus 7.4%) with lower position and orientation errors and tighter bimanual synchronization. Both algorithms degrade on unseen boundary targets, but SAC retains most of its performance while PPO's collapses. The results also expose a failure mode of PPO: under the two-phase shaped reward, it tends to converge to a reward-loitering local optimum rather than committing to the precision task. This behavior highlights the sensitivity of on-policy learning to reward shaping.

Introduction sec:introduction Background and Motivation Orbital debris now poses a major threat to the long-term sustainability, safety, and economic viability of space operations. The accumulation of non-functional satellites, spent launch-vehicle stages, and fragmentation debris has substantially increased the collision risk in low Earth orbit, where a single high-energy collision could trigger a cascading fragmentation process that compromises the usability of critical orbital regions. These concerns have brought active debris removal, on-orbit servicing, and autonomous capture to the forefront of space-safety research.~ flores2014review,fallahiarezoodar2025review Robotic manipulators have emerged as one of the most practical enabling technologies for these tasks. Unlike human-crewed approaches, they interact directly with non-cooperative targets, perform capture and stabilization maneuvers, and operate without exposing astronauts to risk. Dual-arm configurations are particularly promising, since coordinated manipulation distributes contact forces more effectively, improves the ability to secure irregular or tumbling objects, and reduces the likelihood of grasp failure relative to single-arm systems.~ alizadeh2024comprehensive These advantages are especially important when the target provides no dedicated grapple fixture and its motion is only partially known. However, coordinating two manipulators in orbit is difficult. Inter-arm collision avoidance, kinematic redundancy, and the need for smooth, synchronized motion under sensing uncertainty add substantial complexity. Meeting these demands reliably is therefore central to making dual-arm space manipulators practically viable. Related Work Classical nonlinear, robust, and optimal control strategies have been applied to many dynamical systems to mitigate disturbances and modeling uncertainties.~ shi2022robust,11129913,10801815,wang2022robust,WANG202611355,XIE2020156,fallahiarezoodar2024optimal However, these methods typically rely on accurate models and carefully tuned controllers, which limits their adaptability to the highly uncertain, contact-rich capture scenarios encountered in dual-arm operations involving non-cooperative targets. These limitations motivate learning-based approaches, and in particular deep reinforcement learning (DRL), for cooperative motion control of dual-arm space robots. DRL methods can learn coordination policies directly from interaction data, capturing complex contact dynamics, uncertainty, and redundancy without requiring explicit analytic controller design. Among DRL methods, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) represent two widely used paradigms with distinct learning mechanisms, sample-efficiency properties, and exploration strategies. PPO has attracted considerable attention in space-robotic motion planning owing to its stable policy updates, implementation simplicity, and suitability for continuous control. Wang et al. applied a PPO-based strategy to multi-target trajectory planning for a six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) free-floating space robot, demonstrating improved tracking performance and robustness under external disturbances, base-parameter variations, and joint-failure scenarios.~ wang2021multi Reinforcement learning has also been investigated for dual-arm robotic capture of non-cooperative dynamic targets, where sim-to-real transfer improved the practical applicability of the learned capture policies.~ du2023reinforcement More recent studies have extended learning-based motion planning toward dual-arm free-floating space robots and non-cooperative target capture, where coordinated planning must address dynamic coupling, high-dimensional action spaces, and end-effector pose constraints.~ cao2023reinforcement,wang2022learning Nevertheless, because PPO is an on-policy algorithm, it often requires substantial interaction data, and its performance can be sensitive to reward design, network architecture, and hyperparameter tuning. In contrast, off-policy actor--critic methods offer a promising alternative for improving sample efficiency in continuous control. SAC, in particular, incorporates entropy regularization to promote exploration and stabilize learning, making it well suited to high-dimensional continuous action spaces. SAC-based approaches have been applied to robotic path planning and obstacle avoidance, including dynamic obstacle avoidance, multi-arm manipulator path planning, and dual-arm trajectory planning in configuration space.~ prianto2020path,cao2023reinforcement,choi2021reinforcement,li2025deep The most closely related space-robot study jointly incorporates collision avoidance, orientation alignment, and observation-noise robustness for a free-floating manipulator, but does so for a single arm using Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG).~ alali2024rlpath More broadly, prior dual-arm space-robot studies each commit to a single learning algorithm, predominantly off-policy DDPG~ wu2020reinforcement,li2021constrained or PPO alone~ karim2025davil , and none contrast on-policy PPO with maximum-entropy SAC under an identical dual-arm formulation. Contributions Despite this progress, existing learning-based studies rarely address, within a single dual-arm space-manipulator formulation, the joint requirements of target-reaching accuracy, inter-arm collision avoidance, orientation alignment, motion smoothness, and synchronized task completion, while also generalizing to unseen target configurations. Direct comparisons between on-policy and off-policy algorithms under an identical dual-arm task formulation also remain limited, as summarized in Table~ tab:related_work_matrix . To address this limitation, this paper develops a coordinated reinforcement learning framework for cooperative motion planning of a dual-arm space manipulator and evaluates PPO and SAC within the same formulation. Rather than focusing solely on algorithm selection, the proposed approach constructs a task-specific cooperative learning architecture tailored to space-robotic capture operations. The objective is to enable both manipulators to reach their assigned targets while maintaining safe inter-arm motion, satisfying task-level position and orientation requirements, and producing smooth, physically feasible joint-space trajectories. To this end, a centralized state representation combines joint-space states, end-effector kinematics, and target-relative observations, and a multi-objective reward function balances target-reaching accuracy, orientation alignment, motion smoothness, inter-arm collision avoidance, and synchronized task completion. Within this framework, PPO and SAC are employed as representative on-policy and off-policy algorithms to evaluate how different policy-optimization paradigms realize the proposed formulation. The main contributions are summarized as follows: A reinforcement-learning-based formulation is developed for cooperative motion planning of a dual-arm space manipulator in a target-reaching task with inter-arm collision-avoidance constraints. A centralized state representation is constructed by incorporating joint-space information, end-effector kinematics, and target-relative observations to support coordinated dual-arm policy learning. A multi-objective reward function is designed to promote target-reaching accuracy, orientation alignment, smooth joint motion, synchronized task completion, and inter-arm collision avoidance. PPO and SAC are compared as representative on-policy and off-policy DRL algorithms to assess their convergence behavior, task performance, and suitability for the proposed cooperative motion-planning problem. The learned policies are evaluated on unseen target configurations to examine their generalization capability within the considered simulation scenarios. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~ sec:proposed_system describes the dual-arm robotic system and its reachable workspace. Section~ sec:technical_preliminaries reviews the reinforcement learning preliminaries and the PPO and SAC algorithms. Section~ sec:problem_formulation formulates the cooperative motion-planning problem as a Markov decision process, including the state and action spaces and the multi-objective reward design. Section~ sec:simulation_results presents the comparative simulation results for PPO and SAC. Finally, Section~ sec:conclusion concludes the paper and outlines future work. This configuration supports repeated contact and reliable grasping while reducing the likelihood of inadvertently pushing the target away during cooperative manipulation. All motion is confined to a plane: each end-effector position is a two-dimensional coordinate and its orientation a single planar heading angle. The task is target reaching; a completed grasp is not required for success, and the grasp bonus introduced in Section~ sec:problem_formulation is an auxiliary shaping signal. title: Do VLAs Know They Will Fail? Interpretable Success and Failure Patterns in Physical AI Systems

summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as powerful general-purpose robot policies, but their successes and failures remain difficult to diagnose and understand. In this work, we show that sparse autoencoder (SAE) representations of OpenVLA activations contain outcome-predictive information and can be used to predict task failure before the robot reaches an unrecoverable state. Moreover, to provide insights into what common behaviors may contribute to these outcomes, we identify individual SAE features whose strong activations are associated with specific stages of success or failure, and uncover recurring behavioral patterns by localizing temporal intervals where these features exhibit significant activation changes. Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong generalist performance by scaling model capacity and training data~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla , but their internal representations make it difficult to diagnose why a rollout succeeds or fails. Recent work shows that these representations anticipate failure. SAFE learns a multitask failure detector from internal VLA features and uses conformal prediction to trade detection accuracy against warning time~ gu2025safe . Mahato and Ren show that near-term failure is linearly decodable from OpenVLA activations under visual distribution shift~ mahato2026early . FPC-VLA instead predicts failures with an external VLM supervisor~ yang2026fpcvla . These works report warning time relative to the end of the episode. The problem is that every action an agent takes changes how easy the remaining task is to complete; thus, these approaches may trigger an alarm after the task has become unrecoverable. We therefore build on this line of research by measuring lead time against a point of no return, a timestep after which the only reachable states by branched policies are failures. More importantly, we aim to move beyond predicting outcomes toward identifying the behavioral patterns strongly associated with success or failure. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide a promising approach by decomposing dense, polysemantic activations into sparse, potentially interpretable features~ bricken2023towards,cunningham2023sparse . Recent work has applied this technique to VLAs. Haon et al.~ haon2025mechanistic identify interpretable, steerable directions in OpenVLA. Swann et al.~ swann2026sparse find SAE features for motion and semantics, some of which causally steer behavior. Event-Grounded SAEs tie features to behaviorally salient events in closed-loop rollouts~ jin2026eventgrounded . These works characterize features by what they represent or control. We ask a complementary question: which sparse features track whether a rollout will succeed, and what behavior do they correspond to? We show that SAE features preserve the outcome-predictive information in OpenVLA activations, and that, evaluated against the point of no return, the predictor separates eventual failures from successes while the failures are still recoverable. We then select individual features by their association with trajectory outcomes and automatically localize the critical intervals where they emerge. Finally, we describe these intervals with a VLM and validate the descriptions on held-out clips via detection scoring~ bills2023language,paulo2024automatically . Together, these steps connect early failure warning to interpretable, failure-relevant behavior in VLA policies. An extended discussion of related work is in Appendix~ sec:citations-extended . While dense activations may contain outcome-predictive information, their polysemanticity makes it difficult to identify the specific behavioral patterns associated with success or failure~ bricken2023towards,cunningham2023sparse . We therefore use a TopK sparse autoencoder (2 , 048 features, ) to decompose them into sparse feature activations . We ask whether and predict the eventual outcome, and whether individual SAE features reveal interpretable success- and failure-related behavior (task, splits, and SAE details are in Appendix~ app:setup ). Online Outcome Prediction sec:online-prediction We first test whether the raw activations and SAE features contain information predictive of the eventual trajectory outcome. Specifically, at each timestep , we train a logistic regressor using either the raw activations or SAE features to predict the final outcome of an ongoing trajectory, taking its predicted failure probability as . To reduce transient activation noise, we consider activations within a rolling window of steps rather than single-step activations. The predictor input is the rolling mean raw activation or the rolling mean SAE representation . As successful trajectories tend to terminate earlier, the activations at large predominantly come from failed trajectories, causing severe label imbalance and making high accuracy easy to achieve. We therefore compare our predictor with a majority baseline that takes no input and always predicts the majority outcome label at each timestep . Figure~ fig:online-prediction (a) shows that raw activations and SAE features achieve similar accuracy and outperform the majority baseline at early-to-mid timesteps. Their AUROCs are also nearly identical (0.80 and 0.81, respectively, over all held-out frames), remaining above chance from the first 80 steps (0.68) through steps 240-319 (0.75). Predicting failure before an episode ends does not necessarily provide an actionable warning, as the robot may have already reached an unrecoverable state. title: RoboCode: Learning Reusable Action Primitives for Robot Manipulation
summary:
Recent robot manipulation policies commonly predict continuous action chunks directly from observations, without explicitly modeling reusable structure in the action space. However, manipulation demonstrations often contain recurring short-horizon motion patterns that are shared across tasks. We introduce \textsc{RoboCode}, which learns these patterns through a shared soft-gated primitive action interface. Rather than assigning each action chunk to a single discrete code, \textsc{RoboCode} represents it as a soft composition of multiple learned primitives, providing a flexible intermediate representation of short-horizon actions. The primitive interface is learned from action chunks pooled across multiple tasks and then frozen while task-specific state encoders are trained to map current state inputs into the shared latent space.
  Experiments on five ManiSkill manipulation tasks address three questions. First, the learned primitive interface reconstructs action chunks with an average reconstruction MSE of 0.0187. Second, analysis of code activations reveals structured code reuse across tasks. Third, \textsc{RoboCode} achieves the highest or tied closed-loop success rate on all evaluated tasks, with an average success rate of 75.6%, compared with 68.8% for ACT and 41.6% for the larger Diffusion Policy baseline. These results suggest that soft-gated primitive codebooks provide an effective and interpretable intermediate action representation for robot manipulation.

Introduction Robot manipulation is often modeled as a sequence of continuous actions. Across tasks, demonstrations repeatedly contain short motion patterns such as reaching, lifting, placing, and pushing. This suggests that manipulation trajectories may be better understood through reusable primitive structure rather than as independent action chunks. This raises a question of action representation. Recent token-based robot policies discretize each action dimension into bins~ kim2025openvla , offering a simple interface but splitting coordinated actions into dimension-wise decisions. Task-level commands and planning operators~ byrnes2025climb provide semantic structure, but often require a large vocabulary of task-specific actions, limiting generalization across tasks. Primitive-level representations offer a more compositional abstraction, capturing reusable motion units while preserving coordination across action dimensions and time. Prior work has explored reusable units for robot manipulation~ mao2024dexskills,zhu2025learning,lei2026primaryfine , including behavior segments, semantic skill spaces, and discrete action modes. However, a single primitive may not be sufficiently expressive for a short action chunk, since the chunk can contain multiple motion factors. Inspired by memory-augmented models~ gong2019memorizing,yang2021memory , we learn primitive codes as entries in a shared primitive codebook and represent each chunk as a soft composition of multiple entries. We propose , a two-stage framework for learning soft-gated primitive codebooks from robot demonstrations. The first stage jointly learns an action encoder and a shared primitive action interface from multi-task action chunks. The second stage trains task-specific observation-to-gate policies that use this frozen interface to generate continuous action chunks for execution. Our aim is to study whether soft-gated primitive codebooks provide an effective intermediate action representation for robot manipulation. The method does not require manually designed primitives, task rewards, or task labels during primitive learning; it discovers reusable action components directly from demonstrations. Our contributions are: We introduce a soft-gated primitive action representation that represents short-horizon manipulation actions as compositions of multiple learned primitives, rather than direct continuous predictions or single-code assignments. The proposed two-stage framework learns a shared primitive action interface from pooled multi-task demonstrations and reuses the frozen interface for task-specific closed-loop control. Experiments on five ManiSkill manipulation tasks demonstrate structured cross-task primitive reuse. achieves the highest or tied success rate across all evaluated tasks, reaching an average success rate of \(75.6 \), compared with \(68.8 \) for ACT and \(41.6 \) for DP-Large. Controlled ablations and transfer experiments further examine the roles of soft composition and cross-task primitive sharing. Related Work Imitation Learning for Robot Manipulation Imitation learning has become a widely used paradigm for acquiring robot manipulation behaviors directly from expert demonstrations. Many behavior-cloning policies formulate control around predicting a current low-level action from the current observation. Implicit Behavioral Cloning (IBC)~ florence2022implicit , for example, models state--action relationships through an energy-based policy, providing an expressive alternative to explicit action regression. Perceiver-Actor (PerAct)~ shridhar2023perceiver predicts the next discretized 6-DoF action from language-conditioned 3D observations for multi-task manipulation. BC-Z~ jang2022bc extends behavior cloning to large collections of tasks through language- and video-conditioned policies; its closed-loop policy executes the current predicted action while also incorporating future open-loop trajectory prediction during training. More recent methods increasingly model temporally extended actions directly. Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT)~ zhao2023learning predicts sequences of future actions as chunks, reducing the effective prediction horizon for fine-grained manipulation. Diffusion Policy ~ chi2025diffusion models action sequences through conditional diffusion and supports receding-horizon execution. Temporally extended action prediction has further scaled to generalist robot policies: Octo~ team2024octo learns from diverse robot embodiments and tasks, while RDT-1B ~ liu2025rdt employs a diffusion Transformer to model complex action distributions for bimanual manipulation. Together, these developments expand imitation learning from current-action prediction toward joint modeling of temporally extended robot behavior. Beyond predicting such behaviors, a related line of work investigates whether recurring structure within manipulation trajectories can be captured and reused through motion primitives and skill abstractions. Motion Primitives and Skill Learning Motion primitives and skill abstractions organize robot behavior into reusable units between task objectives and low-level control. Hierarchical manipulation approaches decompose multi-phase tasks into reusable skills and learn their selection and adaptation across different phases ~ kroemer2015towards . Other methods define primitives around physical interaction structure. Tactile Dexterity~ hogan2020tactile combines manipulation primitives with tactile feedback for contact-rich manipulation, while HACMan++~ jiang2024hacman++ introduces spatially grounded parameterized motion primitives that combine discrete primitive selection with continuous grounding and execution parameters. Motion primitives have also been integrated with planning and reinforcement learning ~ kicki2024bridging . Recent approaches increasingly learn reusable behavioral units directly from demonstrations or experience. DexSkills~ mao2024dexskills segments long-horizon manipulation demonstrations into skills using multimodal sensory information. XSkill~ xu2023xskill discovers cross-embodiment skill prototypes from unlabeled human and robot manipulation demonstrations and transfers the learned representations to robot control. Mao et al. ~ mao2023learning learn reusable manipulation mechanisms from demonstrations and self-play that can be compositionally integrated into task-and-motion planning. Recent methods further explore semantic and hierarchical manipulation abstractions ~ zhu2025learning,liu2025himacon and object-centric interaction primitives~ pan2025omnimanip . These methods differ substantially in what constitutes a reusable behavioral unit, ranging from parameterized motion primitives to segmented, semantic, and cross-embodiment skills. They nevertheless share the broader objective of capturing recurring structure that can be reused across manipulation behaviors. A further question is how such reusable structure participates directly in policy learning and action generation. Structured Action Representations and Codebooks Recent approaches increasingly incorporate structure into the intermediate representations through which policies generate robot actions. OpenVLA ~ kim2024openvla discretizes individual continuous action dimensions into tokens for autoregressive prediction. FAST~ pertsch2025fast instead encodes temporally extended action sequences into compact discrete tokens through frequency-domain transformation and compression. title: From Tabletop to Walking Bot: Deploying a VLA Model on a Legged Manipulator Robot
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are typically pretrained on broad, diverse datasets and subsequently fine-tuned on a comparatively small dataset tailored to a specific target robot. Such adaptation recipe is now widely established, achieving its most mature results on fixed-base arms due to their static base dynamics and consistent reference frame. Mounting the same arm on a quadruped extends the workspace to the entire floor, but fundamentally changes the embodiment: rather than controlling the arm in isolation, the policy must jointly coordinate base navigation, body posture, and end-effector motion. In this work, we study the practical demands of this embodiment change across data collection, model adaptation, and inference design to achieve closed-loop loco-manipulation on a Unitree Go2 with an AgileX Piper arm. We report the choices that made this real-robot deployment feasible, namely model variant, action horizon, and demonstration conventions, together with a study tailored to a pick-and-place task, separating data coverage from model capacity. We show that expanding demonstration coverage reduces held-out end-effector error by 30%, and incorporating secondary skills (such as pushing rather than grasping) introduces new behavioral modes without degrading baseline performance. Finally, closed-loop real-world experiments show how dataset composition shapes success and failure, validating the pipeline for more complex loco-manipulation.
