Finally, closed-loop real-world experiments show how dataset composition shapes success and failure, validating the pipeline for more complex loco-manipulation. vision-language-action models, legged mobile manipulation, imitation learning, teleoperation, robot learning Introduction sec:introduction Adapting a vision-language-action (VLA) model to a new robot follows a de-facto standard procedure: a policy pretrained on large multi-robot manipulation datasets is fine-tuned on a modest number of demonstrations of the target task, each paired with a language instruction, and the resulting policy is queried at runtime for short sequences of actions. The procedure has proven effective on fixed-base manipulators and, more recently, on wheeled mobile platforms fu2024mobile,MOLMO . Extending from fixed-base to legged manipulators changes two things at once. The first is the workspace of the robot. On a fixed-base setup, everything the robot's policy can reach is set by the arm, and an object placed beyond it is simply unreachable. Mounted on a quadruped, the same arm can reach anywhere the robot can walk, so the policy must first move the body to bring the target within the arm's workspace. The second thing is the commanded action space of the policy. A policy on a fixed-base arm emits arm commands alone, whereas a policy on a legged manipulator must additionally command base motion and body posture while the base keeps its balance. Reaching for an object is therefore an inherently coordinated behaviour in which stepping, body pitch, and arm motion are decided together. Both changes matter at deployment. In our instantiation, instead of joint space commands, the policy output is expressed in the quantities that a pretrained locomotion controller expects, so collection and deployment share the same physical factors, such as control delays, contact, and balance dynamics. Collecting the required coordinated demonstrations is itself not straightforward: existing legged teleoperation systems either instrument the operator with wearable motion capture or delegate part of the base motion to an autonomous policy TeleMAN,honerkamp2024zero . In such cases, decisions about base placement are absent from the recorded data. This extended abstract reports initial work toward carrying a pretrained VLA across this change of embodiment and what the resulting performance appears limited by. The next sections describe: a collection setup in which one operator commands base and arm concurrently through an interface later shared with the policy; the training and inference choices that made the model usable on hardware; and a controlled variation of the training data that separates additional examples of a known behaviour from examples of a new one. We close with an initial deployment on the physical robot and outline how this approach can be expanded toward broader loco-manipulation abilities. Data Collection sec:collection The platform adopted consists of a Unitree Go2 quadruped carrying an AgileX Piper L arm with a parallel gripper, a wrist-mounted RealSense D435 camera, and a D405 mounted on the quadruped's head that provides the forward view of the scene. The target loco-manipulation task consists in picking up a plastic cube and placing it on a colored target area. Instructions are drawn from a template set that varies the verb, the instruction phrasing, and the object color, so the policy is not fitted to a single sentence. A further subset of demonstrations reaches the same goal by pushing the cube rather than grasping it, labelled with goal-oriented phrasings that contain no grasping verb. A single operator collects each demonstration. A second Piper arm serves as a haptic device in a leader-follower pair, whose kinematic configuration is mirrored by the follower arm. Two handheld controllers supply the remaining degrees of freedom: body pitch, yaw, gripper toggling, episode markers, and base velocity. One controller is mounted on the leader-arm handle. The same hand therefore can drive arm motion, gripper, and posture, while the other hand commands base velocity. A bilateral teleoperation coupling between leader and follower arm renders contact cues without force sensors. Driving base and arm concurrently yields coordinated reaching and body placement, avoiding less natural motions derived from interleaving a discrete navigation phase with a subsequent manipulation phase. Demonstrations are recorded at Hz , aligned to the slower Hz head camera against the - Hz wrist camera. The operator and the policy issue the same command, comprising, in order, body-frame base twist, body-pitch reference, six absolute arm joint position targets, and the gripper command. The robot-side stack behind this 11D command interface is identical during collection and deployment, with base state supplied by the onboard MUSE estimator MUSE , base commands entering an arm-aware reinforcement-learning locomotion policy derived from BinWalker turrisi26littercollection , and arm commands executed by the joint-trajectory controller (see ). Representing actions as body-level commands, rather than leg joint references, keeps what the policy must learn at the level of coordinated placement decisions. Moreover, using the same controller for operator and high level policy commands keeps collection and execution consistent. A policy trained on these labels can therefore take the operator's place at this command boundary, with no inverse kinematics or controller retargeting between model and robot. The action labels follow four conventions that make the learned behaviour directly deployable. The base action stores the twist the operator commanded rather than the velocity the robot achieved, so the learned quantity coincides with the quantity the controller expects. Body pitch is recorded in the reference space the controller expects, which allows the policy output to be forwarded without rescaling. Arm targets are absolute joint-position targets, so each prediction overwrites the previous one and errors do not accumulate as they would with relative delta commands integrated over time. The gripper actions encode open-or-closed intent rather than measured gripper opening, which would otherwise record the grasped cube's width instead of the decision to close. Training and Inference sec:training We build on the MolmoAct2 family MOLMO , chosen for its open weights and transparency on training recipe. The models adopt a flow-matching expert action head, producing a chunk of actions per observation. The family also offers a reasoning variant with scene-depth prediction. While it enables extended reasoning, the resulting inference latency is too high for closed-loop control of the quadruped. We therefore fine-tune and deploy the plain model with depth reasoning disabled, using rank-512 low-rank adaptation of the vision-language backbone together with a fully trained action expert on a single GPU RTX 6000 Pro ( GB VRAM). The action horizon is set empirically to balance outdated plans, inference delays, and data characteristics. A common choice is to predict one second of action, discretized into five ms steps at Hz , matching data collection frequency. In our system this horizon produced jerky and imprecise motions because each plan was replaced before the motion could settle. Conversely, fifteen-step plans continued to execute commands that no longer matched the current camera view. Empirically, ten actions at Hz proved a workable middle ground. The arm receives the whole action chunk, a sequence of predicted actions, as one multi-point trajectory to avoid goal preemption, while the base, which accepts only instantaneous commands, is served by a Hz keep-alive thread holding the absolute pitch reference and zeroing velocity between inferences. Experiments sec:experiments Building on the deployment setup established above, we examine how far the instructed pick-and-place behaviour is limited by data. We address it by training on three nested datasets while keeping every other setting fixed. We denote them as: D1, contains 131 grasp episodes; D2, adds grasp episodes from a wider range of starting positions, approach directions, and stances, for 233 episodes; D3, further adds 25 push episodes for a total of 258. The held-out set is reported separately per task: 26 grasp episodes, in-distribution for all three models therefore providing fair comparison, and 5 push episodes, in-distribution for D3 alone. Because mean joint error saturates and ranks checkpoints poorly, we report end-effector error obtained through the kinematic chain, expressed in millimeters and therefore directly comparable to the positioning accuracy required to grasp and place the cube, alongside gripper open/close accuracy and pitch error in degrees. title: MAST-VLA: Skill-Conditioned Adaptation with Trajectory-Affordance Priors for Multi-Skill Robot Manipulation
summary: Generalist robot manipulation requires a single vision-language-action (VLA) policy to execute diverse skills across scenes and instructions. However, current multi-skill VLA policies often leave two aspects of an instruction insufficiently modeled: which primitive skill to execute and where/how to contact and move objects. We propose MAST-VLA (Multi-skill Adaptation with Skill-conditioned experts and Trajectory-affordance priors), a dual-conditioning framework for robot manipulation. MAST-VLA introduces skill-conditioned LoRA Mixture-of-Experts (LoRA-MoE) adapters in the LLM backbone, where skill-query tokens and routing biases guide low-rank expert specialization, and converts a predicted affordance heatmap into a patch-level trajectory-affordance spatial prior for the action head. On the CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D long-horizon multi-skill cross-scene generalization setting, MAST-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching an Avg. Len of 4.65 over five-subtask evaluation sequences. Real-robot multi-skill sequence experiments further validate its deployability under real perception and control noise.

Introduction Vision-language-action models (VLAs) provide a unified interface for language-conditioned robot manipulation by connecting visual perception, language understanding, and action generation~ rt2, openvla, pi0, pi05 . Recent VLA policies show that pretrained multimodal models can be adapted to robot control across diverse objects, scenes, tasks, and embodiments~ roboflamingo, octo, openvla_oft, gr00t_n1 . This capability makes VLAs a promising foundation for generalist robot manipulation, where a single policy is expected to reuse visual-language knowledge while executing and composing multiple manipulation skills~ rt1, openx, bc_z . Despite this progress, multi-skill long-horizon manipulation remains challenging because language-conditioned policies must maintain stable execution across sequential subtasks and skill transitions~ calvin, hulc, hulc_plus, spil . A manipulation instruction requires the policy to infer the intended primitive operation, such as grasping, pushing, rotating, or stacking, while also grounding the contact regions, motion paths, and object interactions required for execution~ cliport, peract, rvt, where2act, vat_mart . These two factors are referred to in this work as primitive-skill semantics and object-interaction semantics. When either factor is insufficiently modeled, errors may accumulate across consecutive subtasks, leading to unstable execution under long-horizon skill transitions~ calvin, hulc_plus, lumos . Existing VLA policies often leave these two forms of grounding implicit in language instructions, visual observations, and low-dimensional action supervision~ openvla, openvla_oft, vla_adapter, x_vla . For skill-level grounding, shared adaptation parameters or task-level lightweight modules may not explicitly align expert capacity with primitive manipulation skills, making it difficult to separate skill-specific action patterns and control preferences within a shared policy~ lora, mixture_of_lora_experts, vla_adapter, coral . For interaction-level grounding, low-dimensional action supervision provides only indirect cues about contact regions, motion trends, and task-relevant geometry, whereas prior manipulation methods have shown the importance of explicit spatial, geometric, or affordance-level signals~ transporter, cliport, peract, rvt, affordance_human_video, robopoint . Thus, multi-skill VLA policies require mechanisms that preserve shared visual-language knowledge while explicitly conditioning adaptation on primitive skills and strengthening action-relevant spatial supervision. To address these limitations, we propose MAST-VLA, a dual-conditioning framework for multi-skill robot manipulation. MAST-VLA combines skill-conditioned LoRA-MoE specialization in the LLM backbone with a trajectory-affordance spatial prior in the action head. In the LLM backbone, skill-query tokens and routing biases condition low-rank expert specialization; in the action head, trajectory-derived affordance heatmaps are converted into patch-level attention biases for action decoding. Together, these two paths reduce cross-skill interference and strengthen interaction-aware action generation. The contributions are summarized as follows: 1) A dual-conditioning VLA framework is proposed for multi-skill robot manipulation, jointly modeling primitive-skill structure and interaction-relevant spatial grounding within a shared policy; 2) Skill-conditioned LoRA-MoE specialization and trajectory-affordance action guidance are introduced. The former uses skill-query tokens and routing biases to condition low-rank expert specialization in the LLM backbone, while the latter converts future gripper motion and scene geometry into heatmap supervision and patch-level spatial bias in the action head; 3) MAST-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance on CALVIN ABC D with an Avg. Len of 4.65 and improves Success@5 from 80.0 to 84.7 . Real-robot experiments, ablations, and visualizations further validate sequential robustness and the complementarity of the two paths. Related Work sec:related_work Generalist VLA Policies for Robot Manipulation. Generalist robot policies and vision-language-action models aim to map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions across tasks, scenes, and embodiments~ rt1, rt2, openx, octo, pi0 . Recent VLA policies transfer pretrained visual-language knowledge to manipulation and support efficient adaptation to downstream robot control~ palm_e, roboflamingo, openvla, openvla_oft, vla_adapter . Action modeling has also evolved from autoregressive action tokens to action chunking, diffusion policies, and fast action decoding~ act, diffusion_policy, fast . These advances provide strong generalist priors, but multi-skill adaptation still often leaves primitive-skill separation and interaction grounding implicit in language-action supervision. MAST-VLA treats multi-skill VLA adaptation as a dual-grounding problem: aligning adaptation capacity with primitive skill structure and grounding action decoding in trajectory-derived interaction geometry. Modular Adaptation and Skill Specialization. Parameter-efficient adaptation methods such as adapters, prompt tuning, and LoRA specialize pretrained models with a small number of additional parameters~ adapter, prompt_tuning, lora . For robot policies, lightweight adaptation modules, action-head adaptation, and task-level LoRA experts improve efficient specialization and can reduce multi-task interference~ openvla_oft, vla_adapter, t2s, coral . MoE and LoRA-MoE methods further increase adaptation capacity through sparse expert routing~ sparsely_gated_moe, switch_transformer, mixture_of_lora_experts . However, existing VLA adaptation methods are mainly single-path or task-level, either sharing the same lightweight update across skills or allocating experts by tasks/domains rather than primitive operations. MAST-VLA uses the instruction-derived primitive skill condition to modulate both input-side skill queries and router-side biases, thereby aligning expertized adaptation capacity with primitive robot skills within a shared VLA backbone. Spatial and Affordance Grounding for Manipulation. Robot manipulation requires spatial reasoning about contact regions, motion paths, and 3D object relations. Prior work improves spatial awareness through transport-based representations, voxel or multi-view policies, and 3D-aware manipulation models~ transporter, cliport, peract, rvt, dp3, robmrag . Recent VLA methods also incorporate 3D representations, spatial projections, or geometry-aware visual features into robot control~ pointvla, geovla, spatialvla, falcon_vla . Another line of work provides explicit spatial cues through affordance learning, interaction-region prediction, or trajectory-conditioned visual prompts~ where2act, vat_mart, affordance_human_video, robopoint, tracevla . Unlike methods that mainly use spatial cues as observation representations, target regions, or input prompts, MAST-VLA converts demonstration trajectories into a dense action-decoding prior and injects the predicted heatmap into action-head attention for multi-skill action generation. title: DynaSlots: Slot-Centric 3D Dynamics Pretraining for Robot Manipulation
summary: Robot manipulation involves localized changes: picking up a cup moves the cup while leaving the surrounding scene largely unchanged. Yet existing 3D visual pretraining methods, including recent dynamics-aware variants, model state transitions at the scene level, compressing the motion of everything in a scene into a single global latent action. This conflates semantically distinct transitions in scenes with multiple moving parts, obscures dependencies between changing regions, and leaves the learned representation vulnerable to task-irrelevant scene content. We introduce DynaSlots, an action-free, label-free pretraining framework that decomposes each point cloud frame into a small set of temporally consistent slots and models dynamics at this per-slot level rather than the scene level. A temporal slot propagation module promotes consistent slot assignments across frames; an inverse dynamics model then extracts one latent action per slot from feature differences, and a diffusion-based forward dynamics model, paired with a self-supervised interaction head, predicts each slot's future state while learning pairwise proximity-and-motion relations. Experiments on Meta-World, Adroit, and a RealMan RM65-B robot demonstrate that DynaSlots outperforms prior scene-level baselines. full_text: Robot manipulation involves localized changes: picking up a cup moves the cup while leaving the surrounding scene largely unchanged. Yet existing 3D visual pretraining methods, including recent dynamics-aware variants, model state transitions at the scene level, compressing the motion of everything in a scene into a single global latent action. This conflates semantically distinct transitions in scenes with multiple moving parts, obscures dependencies between changing regions, and leaves the learned representation vulnerable to task-irrelevant scene content. We introduce DynaSlots, an action-free, label-free pretraining framework that decomposes each point cloud frame into a small set of temporally consistent slots and models dynamics at this per-slot level rather than the scene level. A temporal slot propagation module promotes consistent slot assignments across frames; an inverse dynamics model then extracts one latent action per slot from feature differences, and a diffusion-based forward dynamics model, paired with a self-supervised interaction head, predicts each slot's future state while learning pairwise proximity-and-motion relations. Experiments on Meta-World, Adroit, and a RealMan RM65-B robot demonstrate that DynaSlots outperforms prior scene-level baselines. It achieves superior success rates in simulation and exhibits strong robustness to scene clutter and unseen objects in real-world manipulation. Code is available at https://zhucezhanghao12345-source.github.io/DynaSlots-Anonymous/ . Introduction sec:intro Large-scale self-supervised pretraining has become a primary lever for scalable robot learning. In manipulation, 3D representations are attractive: point clouds expose object geometry in metric space, and policies built on them~ ze2024dp3,shridhar2022peract outperform 2D counterparts with less data. This has motivated a growing line of 3D visual pretraining methods~ pang2022pointmae,yu2022pointbert,zhang2022pointm2ae,zheng2024pointdif,jiang2026slp adapting masked autoencoding~ he2022mae and cross-modal objectives~ afham2022crosspoint to point clouds, initializing policies from representations learned on large unlabeled datasets such as RH20T~ fang2023rh20t and Open X-Embodiment~ embodiment2024openx . However, these methods largely overlook what matters most for control: dynamics. Pretraining objectives based on static appearance capture scene structure but not how it changes, and such representations underperform on manipulation benchmarks that demand understanding state transitions. Recent dynamics-aware pretraining closes this gap~ liang2026afro : an inverse dynamics model (IDM) extracts a compact latent action from feature differences across frames, and a diffusion-based forward dynamics model (FDM) predicts the next state conditioned on it, yielding substantial gains over static pretraining. We identify a limitation of this scene-level formulation: it summarizes an entire point cloud into one global feature and one global latent action, yet manipulation induces localized changes: when a robot picks up a milk carton, the carton moves while the table does not. This formulation presents three potential limitations (Fig.~ fig:teaser a): semantic aliasing, since similar motions in different regions can yield similar global feature differences despite representing distinct transitions; implicit interaction dependencies, since a single global vector does not explicitly represent how changes in one region relate to changes in another during manipulation; and distractor sensitivity, since task-irrelevant scene changes can perturb the global representation. To overcome these limitations, we propose DynaSlots (Fig.~ fig:teaser b), a label-free framework for slot-level dynamics-aware 3D pretraining: the latent action of a transition should be defined per slot, not per scene. DynaSlots decomposes each frame into slots via three components: temporal slot propagation, promoting cross-frame slot consistency rather than letting independent per-frame slot attention~ locatello2020slot reorder slots arbitrarily; an inverse dynamics model extracting one latent action per slot from feature differences; and a cross-slot diffusion forward dynamics model with a self-supervised interaction head, in the spirit of neural relational inference~ kipf2018nri , that recovers a contact and co-motion relation between slots. The framework is trained end-to-end with variance-invariance-covariance regularization~ bardes2022vicreg against an EMA target encoder~ caron2021dino . In summary, the primary contributions of this paper are threefold: We introduce the first slot-based dynamics-aware 3D visual pretraining framework, requiring neither action labels, segmentation ground truth, nor reconstruction supervision. We propose temporal slot propagation and a cross-slot diffusion forward dynamics model with a self-supervised interaction head to maintain cross-frame slot correspondence and capture cross-slot interactions. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of DynaSlots for robotic manipulation. Related Work sec:related 3D Visual Pretraining Self-supervised point cloud pretraining learns transferable geometric representations from unlabeled 3D data. Inspired by masked image modeling~ he2022mae , Point-MAE~ pang2022pointmae reconstructs masked point patches, Point-BERT~ yu2022pointbert predicts discrete patch tokens, and Point-M2AE~ zhang2022pointm2ae extends masked autoencoding to multiple spatial scales. I2P-MAE~ zhang2023i2pmae further incorporates guidance from pretrained 2D models. Other objectives include diffusion-based point recovery in PointDif~ zheng2024pointdif and autoregressive patch prediction in PointGPT~ chen2023pointgpt . CrossPoint~ afham2022crosspoint aligns point clouds with rendered images through contrastive learning, while Uni3D~ zhou2025uni3d aligns 3D features with image--text representations. Structural latent points~ jiang2026slp provide a compact representation for manipulation through latent regularization and rendering supervision. These objectives emphasize spatial structure or cross-modal alignment without explicitly modeling action-dependent temporal transitions. DynaSlots instead uses per-slot dynamics as the pretraining signal for downstream manipulation. Dynamics-Aware Pretraining and Latent Actions Latent-action learning extracts transition representations from videos without requiring physical action labels during pretraining. LAPO~ schmidt2024lawa learns latent actions through joint inverse and forward dynamics modeling, and LAPA~ ye2025lapa uses discrete latent actions to pretrain vision-language-action models. LAOF~ bu2026laof introduces optical-flow constraints, while Bu et al.~ bu2026lam empirically evaluate latent-action design choices. VPT~ baker2022vpt follows a different supervision regime: it trains an inverse dynamics model on action-labeled data before annotating unlabeled videos. Finer-grained alternatives include 3D motion fields extracted from human videos~ yin2025motionfield . For representation pretraining, DynaMo~ cui2024dynamo learns from in-domain visual dynamics, and FVP~ hou2025fvp uses diffusion-based next-point-cloud prediction. AFRO~ liang2026afro , our closest baseline, jointly learns inverse and forward dynamics in a global 3D feature space without action or reconstruction supervision. Other approaches use distinct signals: DynaFLIP~ lee2026dynaflip aligns image transitions, language, and 3D flow; AEM~ zhou2026aem models vision-action histories; and Sparse2Act~ guo2026sparse2act uses end-effector actions to supervise sparse 3D features. V-JEPA~2~ assran2025vjepa2 and 3D Foresight~ he2026foresight further connect visual prediction with planning or policy learning. DynaSlots builds on dynamics-aware pretraining by assigning latent actions to temporally corresponding slots and learning cross-slot relations, replacing AFRO's global transition bottleneck with a structured representation. Slot-Based Representation Learning Slot Attention~ locatello2020slot maps visual features into a set of learned slots through competitive attention. SAVi~ kipf2022savi extends this mechanism to video with recurrent slot updates, and SAVi++~ elsayed2022saviplus uses depth prediction to support learning from more complex videos. SlotFormer~ wu2023slotformer learns temporal dynamics over slot sequences, while DINOSAUR~ seitzer2023dinosaur and SlotDiffusion~ wu2023slotdiffusion improve decomposition and generation through feature reconstruction and diffusion decoding, respectively. In robotic control, FOCUS~ ferraro2023focus and SOLD~ mosbach2025sold explore structured world models for model-based reinforcement learning. Neural relational inference~ kipf2018nri jointly learns latent interaction graphs and dynamics, motivating relational modeling beyond independent slot prediction. Temporal slot consistency and relational dynamics are therefore established ideas. Our focus is their integration with per-slot latent-action learning directly on unordered 3D point clouds, using a pretraining objective that requires neither physical action labels, segmentation labels, nor reconstruction targets. Here, slots form a learned soft scene decomposition and need not correspond one-to-one with physical objects. A Point Transformer first tokenizes each frame. Three modules then model per-slot dynamics: an inverse dynamics model (IDM) extracts latent actions from slot differences; a diffusion-based forward dynamics model (FDM) predicts future slot states; and an interaction head estimates pairwise proximity-and-motion relations. The framework is optimized end-to-end using a VICReg-style loss against a momentum-updated EMA target. title: HGWM: Hierarchical Graph-Guided World Model for Zero-Shot Object Navigation via Graph Matching
summary: Zero-shot object navigation requires an embodied agent to choose where to search while retaining evidence from previous observations. HGWM couples an LLM-generated room-anchor prior with persistent spatial-semantic memory. A coarse stage assigns visual-semantic scores to candidate headings on a 0-10 scale; a fine stage measures symbolic compatibility between observed objects, room context, and the goal prior. Phase-dependent fusion combines these scores with an LLM direction recommendation before local action selection. On HM3D v0.1, the reported HGWM configuration achieves 62.6% success rate (SR) and 31.5% success weighted by path length (SPL), compared with 58.1% and 31.2% for WMNav. On MP3D, the corresponding values are 46.8% and 17.9%, compared with 45.4% and 17.2%. The results indicate higher success point estimates and modest path-efficiency gains. On HM3D v0.2, the full model obtains 74.4% SR and 31.9% SPL. Additional component ablations reduce SR by 0.9-2.3 percentage points and SPL by 0.6-1.5 points. These are author-reported aggregate measurements. The accompanying implementation repairs pass offline tests; episode-level rerun records are not available. Evaluation is confined to simulation.

Evaluation is confined to simulation. ] Introduction Navigation in an unfamiliar environment benefits from both recognizing visible objects and anticipating where a target might be found. Foundation-model agents provide open-vocabulary semantic cues~ yin2025unigoal,nie2025wmnav , but ambiguous observations and incomplete spatial memory can still lead to unproductive search. A useful prior should guide exploration without being mistaken for a verified map of the environment. We study two design challenges: retaining observations across viewpoints and using prior room--object relations to assess candidate directions. VLM detections can be incorrect, while common indoor associations need not hold in every scene. Structural checks may therefore help reject some misleading interpretations but can also suppress valid, atypical observations. HGWM addresses these challenges through a predict-then-ground design. An LLM first generates a hierarchical goal graph describing plausible rooms, anchors, and connections. During navigation, RGB-D observations populate a persistent spatial-semantic graph. Coarse visual-semantic scoring and fine prior-conditioned matching then inform action selection. Here, grounding means relating a hypothesis to sensor-derived evidence, not proving that either graph is correct. A category such as bed specifies no room instance, route, or viewpoint. A room--anchor hypothesis supplies plausible search contexts before the target appears, while memory records encountered evidence. Their compatibility gives relational context a defined role in ranking where to look next. Our contributions are threefold: A symbolic predictive navigation state coupling a hierarchical goal prior with persistent spatial-semantic graph memory. A two-stage decision rule that separates prior-conditioned visual scoring from explicit, direction-specific matching of observed and hypothesized relations. Evaluation on HM3D and MP3D, including four additional component ablations on HM3D v0.2, analysis of success and path efficiency, and qualitative navigation examples. Relative to the reported WMNav results, HGWM improves SR by 4.5 percentage points (pp) on HM3D v0.1 and 1.4 pp on MP3D; SPL improves by 0.3 pp and 0.7 pp, respectively. These are point-estimate comparisons, not evidence of statistical significance. The qualitative trajectories motivate studying repeated exploration, but no aggregate loop-frequency metric is reported. Related Work Semantic search and spatial maps. ObjectNav methods differ in how they represent prior knowledge and retain observations~ sun2024survey,ieong2025multimodal . Habitat-Web and OVRL-V2 learn navigation capabilities from task data~ ramrakhya2022habitat,yadav2023ovrl ; ZSON, CoW, ESC, OpenFMNav, and semantic-frontier approaches exploit pretrained representations or commonsense knowledge~ majumdar2022zson,gadre2023cows,zhou2023esc,kuang2024openfmnav,chen2023not . VLFM accumulates visual-language relevance in a frontier value map~ yokoyama2024vlfm . VoroNav uses a reduced Voronoi graph and path descriptions for waypoint reasoning~ wu2024voronav , while BeliefMapNav estimates target-location belief in a 3D voxel space and plans sequences of destinations~ zhou2025beliefmapnav . Together with 3D-Aware and ApexNav~ zhang20233d,zhang2025apexnav , these systems establish spatial memory and target-directed search as important design choices. HGWM focuses on a complementary question: how a category-conditioned relational hypothesis should influence the score assigned to each candidate heading. Scene graphs for embodied reasoning. SOON, HOZ, and ConceptGraphs use structured scene representations~ zhu2021soon,zhang2021hierarchical,gu2024conceptgraphs . SG-Nav builds an online hierarchy of objects, groups, and rooms, uses hierarchical language-model reasoning, and introduces graph-based re-perception~ yin2024sg . HGWM therefore builds on an established use of graphs for context and perception review. Its specific design couples observed memory with a separate room--anchor hypothesis and makes their compatibility an explicit decision signal alongside visual-semantic scores. The contribution concerns this prior-to-action interface, rather than scene-graph construction alone. Goal graphs and the ObjectNav setting. UniGoal is the closest graph-matching reference~ yin2025unigoal . It unifies object, image, and text goals, matches node and edge embeddings, evaluates graph-edit similarity, and switches exploration strategies according to the matching state. Its paper explicitly notes that an ObjectNav category becomes a single goal node, disabling goal-graph decomposition and anchor-pair alignment in that setting. HGWM expands the category into room hypotheses, anchor objects, and relations before observation. This expansion supplies relational search cues even when the requested goal is only an object category. HGWM then scores headings with explicit symbolic features and phase-dependent fusion; UniGoal uses matched graph structure and, where applicable, anchor alignment to generate exploration destinations. Both use graph matching and staged reasoning, but they differ in the category-goal representation and the mechanism connecting matching to navigation. VLM decision memory. WMNav scores panoramic views, accumulates a curiosity value map, and combines subtask feedback with a two-stage action proposer~ nie2025wmnav . HGWM retains this useful map-and-policy structure while adding a separate goal prior, persistent relational evidence, and a fine compatibility channel. Its decision rule combines visual promise, graph compatibility, and an LLM direction recommendation using coefficients selected from the current matching state. This specifies how graph context changes the input to the stored direction-value map; it does not treat memory or subtask decomposition as new in themselves. Predictive models and HGWM's contribution. SGM predicts missing regions of semantic maps~ zhang2024imagine . World Models, Dreamer, Pathdreamer, and Navigation World Models learn predictive representations of environments~ ha2018world,hafner2023mastering,koh2021pathdreamer,bar2025navigation . HGWM uses pretrained models to form a symbolic hypothesis and compare it with observed evidence, without training a dynamics model or synthesizing future observations. Predictive coding is a conceptual motivation~ friston2010free,clark2013whatever . The methodological contribution is the combination of category-to-graph expansion, direction-specific compatibility, and phase-dependent fusion within persistent decision memory. The experiments distinguish whole-configuration performance from evidence about each component. The Proposed Method HGWM maintains a symbolic predictive navigation state: a goal prior, an observation memory, and scores for candidate headings. The term world model denotes this state, not a learned dynamics simulator. Figure~ fig:architecture shows the perception--memory--decision loop. Section~ sec:reproduction identifies the reported evaluation and available reproducibility records. Task and Decision State The target is an object category . At decision step , the agent receives RGB-D observations and a planar pose . The panoramic scorer uses six relative headings . A high-level decision selects a search direction and a short-horizon subtask; the local navigator then selects a feasible displacement. The 40-step horizon counts agent decision iterations, not a uniform metric distance traveled. Here is a coarse score and is a symbolic compatibility score. Neither is a posterior probability. Success requires the stopping condition within of a target instance under the evaluation protocol, rather than complete alignment of the graphs. Goal Prior and Observation Memory sec:goal_hallucination Given , an LLM returns a structured prior containing likely rooms, alternative rooms, anchor objects, and room connections: This graph is a category-conditioned hypothesis, not a map of the particular scene. In the supplied implementation, priors are cached by goal within an episode and the cache is cleared on reset. We do not assume identical priors across independently executed episodes. What is predicted. The prior describes object categories and plausible relations, rather than asserting coordinates for unseen objects. For example, a bed query can suggest a bedroom and nearby furniture as search context. A detected anchor contributes evidence for a direction even before the bed is visible; failure to observe that anchor is not proof that a bed is absent. Alternative rooms in the prior preserve multiple search hypotheses. Hypothetical nodes are kept separate from observation records so that an expected object is not counted as a detected object merely because the LLM mentioned it. sec:world_model Spatial-semantic memory stores object names, inferred rooms, observation counts, and estimated map positions. The revised implementation queues depth-based navigation rays before the VLM response arrives, then associates each directional description with the nearest available view-center ray within . Projection uses pose, a maximum ray distance of , and map pixels per meter. These are coarse positional estimates for a view, not precise object bounding-box projections. The current local graph additionally uses textual spatial and depth cues. For each direction, current observations and retrieved memory are normalized into one graph contract before matching. It exposes consistent flat and typed views of room nodes, object nodes, adjacency, object relations, and containment. Field aliases are resolved once, objects retain stable identifiers, and observed room membership supplies containment edges. Current attributes take precedence for the same identifier. This boundary prevents a scorer from silently reading a different graph representation. Matching uses symbolic features, without a learned graph-embedding network. Coarse Visual-Semantic Scoring sec:grounding The VLM receives the panorama, goal, and prior context and returns a JSON record per heading with a score, objects, room, path assessment, and explanation: The requested score range is 0--10. This is a model judgment, not a validated detector confidence. title: UAV-SwarmAgent: Scalable Multi-UAV Reconnaissance and Task Allocation via Code Generation and Vision-Language Reasoning
summary: Supervising a multi-UAV reconnaissance mission usually means plotting waypoints and watching every drone. We present UAV SwarmAgent, a hierarchical multi-agent system in which an operator states the mission in one natural-language sentence and a ground-station agent writes and executes code that turns it into per-UAV routes. The agent grounds inspection targets in an aerial map with a vision-language model, splits them among N UAVs by balancing route length, and dispatches worker agents that verify incidents with a compact onboard decision model. In simulation over 4 incident types and 3 foundation models, the swarm located the incident in 244 of 255 missions (95.7%). A paired scaling study with one to 5 UAVs shows that flight time follows an Amdahl-type law. The second UAV delivers half of the attainable saving and the speedup is bounded at 1.52x. We discuss what this predictability, and the false alarms we observed, imply for an operator who supervises the swarm, and outline the user study needed to test it.

Adding drones shortens the mission, but it also multiplies the work of the person in charge: each UAV needs waypoints, and each video stream needs attention. Research on supervisory control has long shown that the number of robots one operator can handle is limited by how long a robot can be neglected relative to how long it takes to service it~ olsen2004metrics,crandall2005validating , and that workload and situation awareness degrade as teams grow~ chen2014human,kolling2016human . Large language and vision-language models offer a different division of labour. They can read a satellite image, follow an underspecified request, and write programs that call tools~ yao2023react,liang2023code,wang2024codeact . Recent aerial systems use them to navigate from language instructions~ liu2023aerialvlnvisionandlanguagenavigationuavs,lee2024citynavlanguagegoalaerialnavigation or to generate a single-drone mission from a map~ sautenkov2025uavvlavisionlanguageactionlargescale,sautenkov2025uavcodeagents . What is missing for human-swarm interaction is the step from one instruction to a multi-drone mission whose duration the operator can anticipate. This late-breaking report presents , a system in which the operator writes one sentence (``I need to check the houses; one of them might be on fire'') and receives the locations of detected incidents with the supporting camera frames (Figure~ fig:teaser ). System sec:system Agents is built on the open-source smolagents library and has two tiers (Figure~ fig:process ). The Airspace Management Agent (AMA) runs at the ground station and works in a ReAct loop whose actions are short Python programs executed in a sandbox: it infers which structures or areas are worth inspecting, grounds them as waypoints on the archival map, shows them to the operator, and dispatches the swarm. One UAV agent per drone runs the onboard verifier on the camera frames collected along its route. We keep geometry out of the language model's hands. Route allocation, flight simulation, and delegation are a single tool call, dispatch swarm, rather than code the model writes itself. In a prototype where the model wrote this code, one model silently rescaled the waypoint coordinates before dispatch, which shifted every route. Fixed tools make the behaviour of the swarm independent of which model plans the mission. Grounding inspection targets The AMA sends the map, letterboxed to a grid, to a vision-language model and asks for waypoints. The prompt distinguishes two kinds of targets. Objects such as buildings or vehicles receive one point at their centre. Areas such as open water or forest receive an even spread of points, because one point in the middle of a lake does not make a drone survey it (Figure~ fig:scenarios ). Returned points are mapped back to map pixels; at most 15 are kept. Answers in which several object points lie on one image axis at equal spacing are discarded as fabricated. Allocating routes Waypoints are assigned to UAVs that start and land at one base station. Because the mission ends when the last drone returns, we balance the longest route rather than the total distance: waypoints are taken farthest-first and each goes to the UAV whose closed route stays shortest after receiving it; each UAV then visits its waypoints in nearest-neighbour order. Verifying incidents onboard Each UAV carries a nadir camera with a \,px footprint (about 170\,m on the ground). A frame is scored every 16\,m along the route by Valen-Preview-0923, a 2B-parameter vision-language decision model that returns the probability of ``yes'' for a scenario-specific question (for example, whether flames or smoke are visible) in a single forward pass, without generating text. At this size the verifier can run locally on the drone, on an embedded NVIDIA Jetson computer; in our experiments it ran on a laptop GPU. title: ACWM-RM: A Reference-Free Reward Model from Complementary Mismatch Preferences
summary: Reinforcement learning has gained attention for improving action-conditioned world models (ACWMs), as it enables reward-driven optimization of visual quality (VQ) and action-following fidelity (AF) beyond flow-matching optimization. Realizing this potential requires reward signals that reliably rank videos by both VQ and AF. However, existing rewards capture only one dimension: metric-based rewards assess VQ but require ground-truth videos and do not directly assess AF, while inverse dynamics model (IDM) rewards assess AF without references but do not guarantee VQ. Moreover, IDMs, typically trained on real videos, may provide unreliable rewards for generated videos containing visual artifacts and physical inconsistencies. In this work, we introduce the Action and Video Mismatch Benchmark (AVM-Eval), comprising 67.2k pairs that evaluate how reliably IDMs assess AF on real and generated videos. We then propose ACWM-RM, a reward model that jointly assesses VQ and AF without ground-truth videos during reward computation. To train it, we first construct the Action and Video Mismatch Preference Dataset (AVM-Pref) with 506.3k pairs providing complementary supervision: action-mismatch pairs supervise AF, while video-mismatch pairs supervise VQ and expose the model to generated videos. We then pretrain an action-conditioned predictor on real videos to learn forward dynamics before jointly training it with a patch-weighted score head on AVM-Pref to transfer these dynamics to AF assessment on generated videos. Evaluation on AVM-Eval reveals the limited reliability of IDMs on generated videos, while downstream RL experiments show that ACWM-RM outperforms reward baselines in both criteria.

For these applications, generated videos must preserve visual quality while faithfully reflecting the commanded actions. However, standard flow-matching training~ lipman2022flow does not explicitly optimize these criteria. This motivates reinforcement learning (RL) such as Flow-GRPO~ liu2025flowgrpo,wu2026roboalign , which optimizes these criteria using rewards. The effectiveness of RL, however, depends on reward signals that reliably rank videos generated under the same conditioning input, assigning higher scores to those with better visual quality (VQ) and action-following fidelity (AF). Existing reward signals fall into two main categories. First, full-reference rewards~ wu2026rlvr use metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, or LPIPS to compare generated videos with the corresponding ground-truth videos, providing VQ supervision but requiring reference videos and not directly assessing AF. Second, inverse dynamics model (IDM) rewards~ seo2026acid,chen2026robotic assess AF without requiring reference videos by comparing actions inferred from generated videos with the input actions used to generate those videos, but do not directly assess VQ. Moreover, IDMs are typically trained on real-world videos, where motion and interactions obey physical laws, but are applied during RL to ACWM-generated videos that may contain visual artifacts and physical inconsistencies, such as robot-arm deformation and interpenetration. To quantify this issue, we generate 100 videos with each of four ACWMs under identical inputs. As shown in Figure~ fig:acwm-consistency , ACWM-generated videos exhibit more visual artifacts and physical inconsistencies than real-world videos. This gap raises the question of whether strong action-mismatch discrimination on real videos translates to reliable assessment of generated videos. In this work, we first construct the Action and Video Mismatch Benchmark (AVM-Eval), comprising 67.2k pairs. It evaluates how reliably IDMs assess AF on real videos using action-mismatch pairs and on generated videos using video-mismatch pairs. We then propose a reward model (ACWM-RM) for jointly assessing VQ and AF without ground-truth videos at reward computation time. To train ACWM-RM, we construct the Action and Video Mismatch Preference Dataset (AVM-Pref) with 506.3k pairs of two types that provide complementary supervision: Action-mismatch pairs contrast original and perturbed actions for the same real video, providing AF supervision; Video-mismatch pairs contrast different generated videos under the same actions, providing VQ supervision while exposing the model to the generated-video distribution. For training strategy, we first pretrain an action-conditioned predictor on features extracted from real robot videos by a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder~ mur2026v , establishing a dynamics representation for AF evaluation. We then jointly optimize the predictor and patch-weighted score head on AVM-Pref, transferring the dynamics learned from real-world videos to AF assessment of generated videos. Our evaluation of four architecturally distinct IDMs on AVM-Eval shows that accurate AF assessment on real videos does not ensure reliable AF evaluation of generated videos. The best-performing IDM achieves 86.1 accuracy on action-mismatch pairs from real videos but only 70.0 on video-mismatch pairs from generated videos. To evaluate ACWM-RM’s downstream effectiveness as an RL reward, we fine-tune DreamDojo-2B with Flow-GRPO, comparing ACWM-RM against the best-performing IDM on AVM-Eval, a metric-based reward, and a VLM-based reward. On held-out tasks, ACWM-RM yields the best VQ and AF, while maintaining VLM-assessed physical consistency (PC) scores close to the original model before RL fine-tuning. (2) We develop AVM-Pref and ACWM-RM, combining dynamics pretraining with complementary mismatch preferences to assess both criteria without references during reward computation. (3) We demonstrate that ACWM-RM outperforms reward baselines in VQ and AF when used for RL fine-tuning. related work Action-Conditioned World Models Action-conditioned world models generate videos conditioned on past observations and actions, simulating the resulting robot interactions to support policy evaluation and planning. To learn transferable dynamics, DreamDojo~ gao2026dreamdojo pretrains on human videos using continuous latent actions and adapts to target robots with robot data. title: Monte Carlo-Based Indoor UAV Localization in Dynamic Environments Using Only Four Onboard Range Sensors
summary: Indoor UAV localization with minimal onboard sensing remains challenging, particularly in dynamic environments. We propose augmented filtered Monte Carlo localization (AF-MCL) for 2D localization using only four single-point range sensors and measured heading. AF-MCL rejects range measurements inconsistent with the known static map and adaptively injects particles to recover from localization divergence and kidnapping. Beam classification is performed only at the previous position estimate, making its ray-casting cost independent of the particle count. The particle distribution additionally provides an online measure of localization uncertainty. Real-world experiments in a 2.10x1.63 m environment yield mean position errors of 6.4-7.7 cm under static and dynamic conditions. Simulations in 6x6 m and 10x10 m environments yield 4.5-5.2 cm mean errors; under dynamic obstacles, standard MCL reaches 12.3 cm and reliable MCL 7.7 cm. The results show that robust indoor localization under dynamic obstacles is achievable with only four single-point range measurements and heading.

Introduction Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly deployed for inspection, inventory monitoring, environmental sensing, and search-and-rescue missions. Their operation indoors requires accurate and low-latency localization despite confined geometry, clutter, and the absence of a reliable global positioning signal~ heidari2023machine,boursianis2022internet, ferreira2017localization,wu2023flytracker . Existing indoor localization solutions typically trade sensing and computational complexity for accuracy. UWB-based methods require external infrastructure and remain sensitive to multipath and non-line-of-sight conditions~ zhao2022finding,hashim2023uwb, nguyen2021range , while vision- and LiDAR-based approaches provide rich environmental information at higher sensing and computational cost~ akai2023reliable,he2022vision,lu2019l3, zimmerman2022robust,nguyen2025uloc . Visual-inertial methods reduce dependence on external infrastructure but accumulate drift, motivating fusion with additional sensing modalities~ wu2023flytracker, chen2024refloc,jiang2024robust . These limitations motivate localization using the sparse, lightweight range sensing available on small UAV platforms. A closely related approach is~ muller2023fully , which performs onboard Monte Carlo localization on a nano-UAV using a pair of 64-zone time-of-flight (ToF) sensors and a parallel ultra-low-power processor. Although computationally efficient, each multizone sensor provides substantially more spatial information than a single-point range measurement, and the method is evaluated in static environments. The problem considered here is therefore more sensing-constrained: can reliable indoor localization be achieved from only four single-point range measurements and heading when individual measurements may also be corrupted by unknown moving obstacles? We address this problem using four single-point range sensors oriented front, back, left, and right. The UAV position is estimated relative to a known initial position in a known static map, using the four range measurements and measured heading . Unknown dynamic obstacles may enter the sensor beams and generate ranges inconsistent with the static map, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:problem_def . No external localization infrastructure is used. To address this setting, we propose AF-MCL. AF-MCL identifies and rejects range measurements inconsistent with the static map before particle weighting, and adaptively injects particles when filter divergence is detected. Crucially, beam classification is evaluated only at the previous position estimate rather than independently at every particle, eliminating particle-count dependence from the classification ray-casting stage. The particle distribution additionally provides an online measure of localization uncertainty. The contribution is threefold. First, we demonstrate 2D indoor UAV localization using only four single-point ranges and measured heading under both static and dynamic obstacles. Second, AF-MCL combines dynamic-beam filtering with adaptive particle injection for robustness to corrupted measurements and localization failures, while requiring only one classification ray cast per sensor, independent of the particle count. Third, simulation and real-world experiments evaluate the contributions of filtering and augmentation, recovery from kidnapping, computational scaling, retained-beam geometry, and localization performance. title: Predictive Long-Horizon Progress Modeling with Action-Aware Quantification
summary: Quantitative and dense task progress feedback is essential for robotic manipulation across data curation, policy evaluation, and reinforcement learning. Existing progress annotations often rely on sparse keyframe markings derived from subjective manual judgments, limiting their scalability and cross-task consistency, particularly in long-horizon manipulation. To overcome these challenges, we propose action-aware quantification, a unified progress specification that decomposes long-horizon trajectories into object-level subtasks via a vision-language model (VLM) and assigns weighted action credits to capture fine-grained execution dynamics. Using VLM auto-labeling and human calibration, we construct an 800+ hour training video dataset and LOOM, a long-horizon progress benchmark containing 19,618 human-calibrated evaluation frames. To model these dense progress dynamics, we introduce NimCritic, a predictive progress critic trained via Joint Video-Progress Learning. We further incorporate Historical Progress Perturbation to mitigate sequential drift, and design a contrastive Video-Progress Alignment objective that bridges asymmetric expert streams by mutually grounding intermediate visual dynamics and denoised progress trajectories. NimCritic matches or outperforms state-of-the-art process reward models (PRMs) on the established Video Progress Benchmark (VPB) and LOOM, surpassing GVL (GPT-6-Sol) on VPB by about 65% in terminal success accuracy (TSA). On the large-scale RoboArena policy evaluation benchmark, it also retrieves human-selected successful rollouts with about 97% overall recall. These results establish action-aware quantification as a scalable foundation for dense progress feedback in robotic manipulation.
full_text: Introduction sec:introduction Process reward models (PRMs) evaluate intermediate execution states from visual observations, supplying dense feedback for robotic data curation, policy evaluation, and reinforcement learning~ robo_dopamine,vlac . Consider a robot instructed to stack blocks in sequence: a completed placement advances the task, an attempted grasp earns temporary partial credit, and a dislodged block triggers revocation of its earlier placement credit. Faithful process supervision must track these state changes across hesitation, progress regression, and recovery. Recent methods draw on vision--language model (VLM)-based reward learning to bring task semantics to visual evaluation, and on video world models to supervise temporal dynamics through future prediction~ liv,wvm . Current PRMs learn relative progress through trajectory comparisons~ robometer , interpolate across manually annotated task stages~ sarm , or assign VLM-generated subtask budgets~ procvlm . Relative comparisons establish trajectory ordering while leaving cross-task progress magnitude unspecified, and elapsed-time interpolation varies with execution speed for the same achieved state~ sarm . Long-horizon feedback must also quantify what a partial attempt contributes and which credit is revoked when a later action destroys an earlier achievement. Scaling process evaluation thus requires both a unified absolute progress specification and a critic that tracks non-monotonic execution across subtasks. To overcome these challenges, we propose action-aware quantification. We first define a subtask as a sequence of operations on the same manipulated object. We then allocate a fixed local budget using the weights of executed actions and the necessary remaining actions. Action boundaries locate the curve breakpoints, and retained weighted action credit determines local progress within this budget. Forward effects receive full credit, engaged-only attempts receive temporary half credit, and subsequent revocations remove the credit of the referenced earlier occurrence. Finally, global progress tracks retained contributions across subtasks, including credit revoked by later destructive actions. VLM pre-annotation and human verification establish structured action records, from which rule-based post-processing computes dense progress for training and evaluation. We assemble a training dataset of 253,276 episodes spanning 800+ hours of robot and human video, together with LOOM (a LOng-hOrizon Manipulation progress benchmark), comprising 300 cross-embodiment trajectories evaluated at 19,618 human-calibrated frames. The benchmark follows successive subtasks in long-horizon execution, covering different rates of advancement, hesitation, regression, recovery, and incomplete execution. Building on this foundation, we introduce NimCritic (A Nimble Critic via Joint Video--Progress Learning), a dual-diffusion-transformer world reward model with separately supervised progress and completion outputs. We term the model nimble because it uses predictive video learning during training and scores subtasks in parallel at inference~ yuan2026fastwam , and a critic because it evaluates task advancement and goal satisfaction. Joint Video--Progress Learning models how the observed state evolves while tying those transitions to advancement toward the specified subtask goal, complemented by Historical Progress Perturbation to regularize sequential history conditioning and contrastive Video--Progress Alignment to strengthen cross-modal correspondence. On the established Video Progress Benchmark (VPB), NimCritic achieves 0.77 overall PRC-F1 and 0.82 TSA (surpassing GVL with GPT-6-Sol by about 65 ). On LOOM, it leads all external baselines across all four metrics in the overall and multi-task groups (0.86 and 0.95 PRC-F1), and on RoboArena it retrieves human-selected successful rollouts with 96.72 overall recall and 98.09 hit rate. We summarize our main contributions as follows: 1pt 0pt 0pt We formulate action-aware quantification, which converts object-level action effects into dense progress through weighted credits, explicit revocation, and composition across complete and incomplete subtasks. We construct an 800+ hour action-aware training dataset through VLM pre-annotation and human verification, and LOOM, a 300-trajectory benchmark with 19,618 human-calibrated evaluation frames for testing long-horizon progress through hesitation, regression, recovery, and incomplete execution. We propose NimCritic, which combines predictive video learning with progress and completion supervision, using Historical Progress Perturbation and Video--Progress Alignment to support sequential estimates and connect visual features to task progress. We demonstrate the highest overall PRC-F1 and TSA on VPB and LOOM, together with 96.72 successful-rollout recall on RoboArena, and analyze the roles of egocentric human videos, non-expert trajectories, and predictive supervision. Related Work sec:related-work Robotic Process Reward Models. Robotic PRMs map visual observations and task instructions to dense intermediate evaluation signals. One line of research builds on vision--language representations: language--image alignment provides goal-conditioned rewards~ liv , while training-free methods infer progress from shuffled frame ordering or completion-token probabilities~ gvl,topreward . Learned VLM critics further supervise relative progress via history-conditioned trajectory comparisons or signed temporal-warp objectives~ robo_dopamine_2,warp_rm , or elicit goal-conditioned process reasoning through reinforcement learning~ primo_r1 . Another line of work predicts alternative quantities such as temporal distance to completion~ rynnvalue or action values for the current subtask~ seeq , alongside benchmarks examining partial observations and multi-stage execution~ opengvl,progresslm . title: When Human Corrections Travel: Safety in Federated VLA Adaptation
comment: Accepted for presentation at SPAIS workshop in CoRL 2026
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can adapt to local human intervention, while federated learning can combine distributed robot experience without pooling raw records. We examine their prospective intersection: sharing adaptations derived from diverse human corrections across tasks, environments, people, and robot embodiments. Corrections differ in modality, safety semantics(urgency, behavioral scope, etc.), and privacy sensitivity. A shared update that improves mean task success may suppress a rare safety intervention or produce an unsafe response on another robot. We argue for three requirements: preserve the context and uncertainty of multimodal corrections when deciding what to share; assess candidate updates in each receiving robot's closed loop before deployment; and evaluate leakage alongside retention of safety-critical evidence. Immediate, legible defensive behavior remains necessary during human interaction. We offer counterexamples and a falsifiable evaluation agenda, not experimental results.

Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and language instructions to robot actions~ zitkovich2023rt2 . Local robot policies can learn from human intervention and online correction~ jiang2025transic,chen2025mereq ; UniSteer specifically adapts a VLA using human takeover actions~ lu2026unisteer . In parallel, FedVLA and ForgeVLA show ways to learn from distributed VLA task data without centralizing raw interaction records~ miao2025fedvla,zhou2026forgevla . A recent study of federated VLA fine-tuning reports that cross-site heterogeneity is more pronounced on physical robots than in its simulations~ duan2026empirical . These strands motivate a prospective setting: robots learn locally from human corrections, then selectively share resulting adaptations. The cited federated systems do not establish the safety of federating multimodal corrections. Such feedback is heterogeneous in ways that task labels do not capture. People may signal a similar intended change by speech, gesture, guided motion, or teleoperation, with different urgency and precision. Consider two sites where a human helps a robot insert a panel. At one site, an operator standing beside the fixture points to a narrow gap and says bring it through here; the pointing gesture performed near the intended path clearly resolves an ambiguous verbal reference. At another site, an operator farther from the fixture gives a detailed verbal description or draws the desired trajectory on a camera image. The reliability of pointing changes with distance, while a drawn 2D route alone may leave depth, contact force, and handover timing unspecified weerakoon2020gesture,mehta2025l2d2 . Each correction may improve its local policy, but their learned effects are not interchangeable. At a receiving site with a rotated fixture, different gripper, or different human hand position, a shared update could reduce clearance or release a jointly held panel too early. A learned motion may also behave differently with another gripper, compliance controller, or action decoder. Federated optimization can encounter client distribution shift and conflicting updates; in embodied systems, a regression can increase contact force, delay a yield, or leave a shared load unsupported. A successful average trajectory offers little evidence about a rare, hazardous interaction. Updates can also reveal private training information even when raw observations remain local~ zhao2024leakage . Our question. What and how may robots learn from diverse, multimodal human corrections across sites, and when may that learning safely change another robot's behavior? Consider a person and robot jointly inserting a panel. A spoken wait, a raised hand, and physical guidance might all signal a needed hold, but they may refer to different hazards or changes in task goal. The source robot can learn useful timing; a receiving robot with a different grip and fixture could release too early. We argue that corrective experience should travel only with a justified scope, receiving-site safety assessment, and an explicit privacy risk assessment. We develop three positions and an evaluation agenda rather than a new algorithm or empirical result. Diverse corrections require scoped transfer Each site adapts a pretrained VLA from locally collected interactions, which may include speech, pointing, drawn routes, physical guidance, and overrides. Sites may share selected learned updates while retaining robot-specific perception and control components. Before an update is transferred, its source context and intended behavioral change need to be identified: did the person specify a goal, a route, a constraint, or an immediate intervention? The receiving robot must then assess whether the learned change has the intended physical effect in its own task and embodiment. A correction can target the current action, future trajectory, goal, safety constraint, or operator preference. Its channel alone does not determine its meaning. Even the same command, such as move left, can mean avoiding a hand, clearing a fixture, or satisfying a local preference. Position 1: share corrections according to behavioral scope, not just parameter compatibility. A proposed update should carry or be evaluated against the source modality, relevant task and human context, intended change, uncertainty, and permitted sharing scope. This is a requirement for accountable adaptation, not a claim that intent can already be inferred reliably or that raw interaction records must leave a site. A guided trajectory may be informative about one robot's geometry while a spoken stop may impose an immediate constraint with little reusable trajectory data. Converting takeover actions into training targets, as UniSteer does~ lu2026unisteer , does not by itself resolve whether an intervention was a safety veto, task correction, or preference. Multimodal federated learning addresses clients that hold different or missing modalities, mainly by aligning or ensembling representations~ feng2023fedmultimodal,yu2023multimodal,ouyang2023harmony . Such alignment can make a spoken stop and a raised hand close in embedding space without establishing that they impose the same constraint; modality heterogeneity in corrective feedback is a question of both meaning and representation. When that distinction cannot be supported, retaining the correction locally is a valid decision. A robot must respond to an urgent intervention before any learning or sharing step. In a joint task, that may mean supporting a load, reducing force, yielding control, or making its defensive state legible to the collaborator. Legibility and perceived safety have established HRI precedents~ dragan2013legibility,tusseyeva2022perceived ; cues should reflect the actual control state. Multiple intervention channels also matter when speech, gesture, or physical guidance is unavailable to a particular person or in a noisy task. These interaction requirements define what future adaptations must preserve, although their detailed design is beyond this paper's scope. Transfer safety is a receiving-site property A feasible design shares some policy components while retaining local action mappings; FedVLA uses personalized components~ miao2025fedvla , and Align-Then-stEer aligns distinct action spaces for cross-embodiment adaptation~ zhang2026ate . Neither parameter separation nor action alignment proves that a correction will transfer safely. The source and receiver may differ in task, hazard geometry, human proximity, dynamics, and intervention protocol. The unit to assess is the receiver's adapted closed-loop system: perception, policy, action mapping, physical safeguards, and human responses. Position 2: a shared update needs a recipient-specific safety gate. Before deployment, a receiver could stage the candidate update and compare it with its current policy from matched local states. An action-conditioned world model could simulate both policies under candidate hazards. SafeDojo uses imagined VLA trajectories to estimate reward and collision cost for safe policy optimization~ tang2026safedojo ; using such rollouts for federated update acceptance is our proposal, not a result of that paper. The comparison should include contact and force, load support, task progress, interruption response, and legible yielding. Simulation alone misses unmodeled dynamics and human reactions, so false acceptance must be measured against local constraint tests and, where appropriate, supervised physical trials. A receiving robot should reject or roll back an update that worsens its safety cases. Local rejection does not remove a harmful contribution already in the shared model; that requires federated unlearning~ liu2021federaser,halimi2022federated . Because approximate unlearning can leave residual behavior, removal should be verified by the same receiver-side safety tests rather than by parameter distance alone. Report the worst-affected receiver as well as mean task success; independent runtime safeguards remain essential~ tolle2025safe . A transfer counterexample. Robot A receives physical guidance away from a person's hand during panel insertion. Robot B completes many uncomplicated insertions and receives only success reports. Robot C, with another gripper and work height, receives a verbal request to slow down, which might be a local preference or a needed contact constraint. An aggregate could improve mean insertion success while weakening A's avoidance response or exporting C's timing to a robot for which it is unsafe. This is a thought experiment, not a finding about a particular aggregation method. The task label and parameter shape do not establish that the underlying corrective experiences are interchangeable. Faulty interpretations and malicious or corrupted client updates create further integrity risks. Privacy mechanisms that hide individual updates may make anomalous contributors harder to inspect; model poisoning work demonstrates this tension in federated learning~ bagdasaryan2020backdoor . Receiving-site validation should therefore test the behavioral consequence, regardless of whether the aggregate appears statistically typical. Privacy must preserve safety-critical evidence Corrections may reveal a goal, a workspace detail, habitual action, or a person's difficulty. Storing raw feedback locally does not rule out inference from transmitted parameters or auxiliary statistics~ zhao2024leakage . A compact update is not a privacy guarantee. Clipping and noise need a defined protection unit, adversary, and privacy accounting; secure aggregation limits server visibility but does not validate the resulting behavior. Position 3: evaluate privacy and safety jointly when deciding what to share. A rare correction may be unusually revealing and unusually important for avoiding harm. Protecting it may erase a safety signal; sharing it unprotected may expose the person or scene. Compare attack success at recovering goals or attributes, retention of safety-critical events, and receiver-side constraint violations at stated protection settings. Highly specific corrections may remain local, with only compatible, lower-risk evidence shared. These are design options to test, not claims of achieved privacy. Risk-aware safety assurance For each correction-derived update, an inspectable record would state the source channel and context, the robot's immediate response, the proposed behavioral change and uncertainty, what leaves the client, and the receiver's acceptance tests and rollback condition. Such a record need not contain raw speech or video and cannot certify safety. It makes the reasons for sharing, withholding, or accepting an update explicit. Position 4: Risk and evidence-aware safety assurance. Comparisons should keep the pretrained policy and safety scenarios fixed while varying modality, task context, embodiment, and sharing strategy. title: If at First You Don't Succeed, Backtrack: Lightweight Recovery for Frozen VLAs
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models perform well on robotic manipulation, yet remain brittle once their own actions carry them into states their training data barely covers. Recovering from such failures usually requires recovery demonstrations, policy retraining, or a separate model at inference time. We introduce Backtrack, a lightweight failure detection and recovery mechanism for frozen VLAs that needs none of these. A small failure prediction head, trained only on outcome-labeled rollouts of the frozen policy, reads the VLA's existing internal representations to estimate whether the current episode will fail. When the predicted failure probability exceeds a threshold, a controller pauses the policy, retraces the arm's recently achieved motion, and hands control back to the unchanged policy so it can retry from an earlier configuration. The head adds only 0.48-0.88% to the policy's parameter count. We evaluate Backtrack on LIBERO with three VLAs spanning two action-generation families: SmolVLA and $π$0.5, which use flow-matching action experts, and the autoregressive $π$0-FAST. On LIBERO-Long, the suite of long-horizon multi-step tasks and the one on which all three policies fail most often, Backtrack reduces each policy's failure rate by 19-48%, raising success by up to 7.4 percentage points; on the three shorter suites, where control success is already 85-99%, its effect is smaller. On MetaWorld, all twelve controller configurations tested with SmolVLA improve on the unassisted policy.
