Introduction Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have spurred the development of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models black_05_2025, pertsch_fast_2025, shukor_smolvla_2025 . These models typically use pretrained VLMs as a backbone, leveraging their visual and language representations to condition the generation of robot actions. Yet even large VLAs trained on diverse, multi-embodiment robotics datasets remain brittle outside their training distribution: modest changes to camera viewpoint, robot initialization, or scene composition can sharply reduce success rates fei_libero-plus_2026 . This challenge is particularly relevant for compact VLAs such as SmolVLA, whose VLM backbone benefits from broad vision-language pretraining, but whose robotics training consists of fewer than 30,000 episodes of community-contributed demonstrations collected primarily on a single robot embodiment shukor_smolvla_2025 . Out-of-distribution states are not only something a VLA encounters; they are also something it can create. Robot imitation datasets are built primarily from successful demonstrations and contain comparatively little data showing how to recover once something has gone wrong dai_racer_2025, shukor_smolvla_2025 . For instance, when a VLA drops an object, knocks something over, or otherwise makes a mistake, it can therefore place itself in a state poorly represented in its training data. Simply allowing more execution time leaves most failures unresolved: on LIBERO-Long, doubling the episode step budget increases success by only 2.3--3.7 percentage points across the three evaluated VLAs (Appendix~ app:budget ). One remedy is to give the policy the data it is missing: collect demonstrations of failures and their recoveries, then train on them dai_racer_2025 . But collecting recovery data is expensive, and the cost may need to be paid again for every new embodiment and task. Instead, we ask whether part of the distribution shift can be reversed directly. After a mistake, both the scene and the robot may have changed: objects may have been displaced, while the arm has moved into an unfamiliar configuration. Changes to the scene are difficult to undo, since restoring a displaced object is itself a manipulation problem. The arm configuration, however, is under our control. This suggests a simple recovery strategy: retrace the arm's motion along the path that led to failure, in the hope of returning toward an earlier configuration from which the unchanged policy can successfully retry. In this work, we introduce Backtrack, a lightweight failure detection and recovery mechanism for frozen VLAs (Figure~ fig:backtrack-overview ). Similar to SAFE gu_safe_2025 , a small failure prediction head reads features the policy has already computed and estimates the probability that the current episode will end in failure; when that probability exceeds a threshold, a controller retraces the arm's recent motion and returns control to the policy. The only supervision Backtrack needs is whether autonomous rollouts of the frozen policy succeed or fail: no teleoperated recovery demonstrations, no policy retraining, and no second model at inference. The head adds just 0.48--0.88 to the policy's parameters. We evaluate Backtrack on three policies with two different action-generation mechanisms: SmolVLA shukor_smolvla_2025 and 0.5 black_05_2025 use flow-matching action experts, while 0-FAST pertsch_fast_2025 generates discrete action tokens autoregressively. On LIBERO-Long liu_libero_2023 , the suite on which all three policies fail most often, Backtrack reduces failure rates by 19 to 48 ; averaged over all four LIBERO suites, the reduction is 20--26 . On MetaWorld yu_meta-world_2020 , where we evaluate SmolVLA on a second benchmark with a different embodiment, all twelve controller configurations we test improve on the unassisted policy. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models VLAs adapt a pretrained vision-language backbone to output robot actions, inheriting its scene and instruction understanding brohan_rt-2_2023, kim_openvla_2024 . They differ in how actions are produced. One family attaches a separate action expert trained by flow matching or diffusion and cross-attending to the backbone, as in SmolVLA shukor_smolvla_2025 and 0.5 black_05_2025 . The other discretizes actions into tokens that the backbone emits autoregressively, as in 0-FAST pertsch_fast_2025 . A parallel line of work develops compact VLAs and backbones for more efficient deployment shukor_smolvla_2025, wang_vla-adapter_2025, marafioti_smolvlm_2025 . Backtrack attaches to a frozen checkpoint and is agnostic to the action-generation architecture; we evaluate it on both families. Failure Detection for VLAs Several lines of work detect signs of failure during policy execution. One uses a separate vision-language model as a judge, either to classify success du_vision-language_2023 or to reason about what went wrong duan_aha_2025, liu_reflect_2023 . Another uses signals derived from the policy itself: agia_unpacking_2025 monitor consistency and progress at runtime, while SAFE gu_safe_2025 trains a lightweight classifier on the policy's internal features and shows transfer across tasks and policies, including 0-FAST, but stops at detection. Backtrack builds on this latter approach: we use the prediction to trigger a lightweight recovery controller, measure what that intervention is worth across three policies, and test whether the effect transfers to a second benchmark. Failure Recovery for VLAs Detection alone does not change the outcome of an episode; something must be done once a failure is predicted. Retrying after a detected failure is not new. Bellman-Guided Retrials du_err_2024 monitors progress with a value function trained on demonstrations and resamples a strategy from the base policy when progress stalls, biasing away from behaviors that have recently failed. Other work prompts a language model to reason its way to a corrective plan lin_failsafe_2025, liu_reflect_2023 . These approaches introduce additional learned components or demonstrations to decide how to recover, but they do not provide a task-agnostic mechanism for returning the robot to a prior configuration while leaving the base policy unchanged. Backtrack instead uses a task-agnostic recovery primitive that requires no recovery demonstrations or learned recovery policy: the controller retraces the arm's recent motion and then returns control to the unchanged VLA. Method sec:method Failure Prediction Head sec:head We attach a Failure Prediction Head (FPH) to the frozen policy. The FPH is a multi-head attention pooling (MAP) layer over the policy's own token features, followed by a three-layer feed-forward network (FFN) that outputs a single scalar: the predicted probability that the current episode will end in failure. Where the features come from. The FPH consumes activations the policy already computes during normal action generation, so it requires no additional forward pass through the backbone. We consider three feature taps: the prefix embeddings the VLM takes as input (pre), the VLM's output representation of that same prefix (post), and post concatenated with the action expert's own hidden states (post expert). Unless stated otherwise, all reported results use post. 0-FAST has no separate action expert: the VLM emits the action tokens itself. Its pre tap is the same as for the other two policies, the prefix embeddings the VLM takes as input. Its post tap is the VLM's representation of that prefix after the prefill, just before the first action token is generated. Parameter overhead. The head is evaluated once per action chunk and reuses activations already present in the forward pass, so its only marginal cost is the MAP layer and the FFN. Its size depends on the width of the features it reads rather than on the size of the policy, so the relative overhead is largest on the smallest policy: it adds at most 0.88 of the policy's parameters, on the 450M SmolVLA, and as little as 0.48 on the 3.6B 0.5 (Table~ tab:head-cost ). Training. The head is trained on rollouts of the frozen policy, with each frame labeled by the outcome of the episode it belongs to. Rollouts are collected across all four LIBERO suites, and we sample with equal weight over the eight (suite, label) cells rather than from the natural distribution. This matters because failures are distributed very unevenly across suites: for 0-FAST, LIBERO-Long supplies 56 of all failure frames and LIBERO-Object only 7 , and the imbalance is larger still for SmolVLA. Sampling from the raw distribution would give one head per policy that is effectively specialized to the suite its policy fails on most, whereas we want a single head that serves all four. The amount of rollout data available differs across policies; Table~ tab:headdata summarizes the rollout pools used for each head. We train each head for 20 , 000 steps with Adam, batch size 32, learning rate and weight decay , with no additional positive-class weighting on top of the balanced sampler. Backtracking Trigger. The intuition is that retracing the arm may undo part of the deviation that led to failure, returning it toward a state better represented in the policy's training data. title: When to Stop Penalizing Actions? Martingale GRPO for VLA Reinforcement Learning
summary: A failed vision-language-action (VLA) rollout does not imply that every action contributed to failure. Yet in group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), a single trajectory-level advantage is assigned to all actions in a rollout. Potentially useful recovery attempts can thus be penalized alongside the errors they aim to correct. Ideal stopping conditions for failure feedback are characterized using success-probability and policy-score martingales. At these stops, the removed gradient contribution has zero conditional expectation given the retained information. Truncation therefore preserves the expectation of a reference GRPO group-gradient estimator and can reduce its covariance. One such stop occurs when the conditional probability of success is zero, motivating error and recovery cues for selecting candidate feedback boundaries. Martingale GRPO (MART-GRPO) is introduced with a vision-language model (VLM) for event-guided truncation. The VLM is fine-tuned on our annotated training set using low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The last visible error without observed recovery is localized by the frozen VLM in complete rollout videos. Failure feedback is retained through the selected error interval and removed afterward, while successful-rollout loss terms and original loss normalization are preserved. For retrospective boundaries, changes in expectation and variance are analyzed to assess departures from ideal stopping. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on RoboTwin 2.0 show that MART-GRPO improves success rates over full-trajectory GRPO across multiple tasks.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to actions~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2025openvla . Pretrained policies are adapted through supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations~ kim2025oft and further optimized through reinforcement learning from environment interaction~ lu2025vlarl,liu2025rlvla . Group-relative policy optimization (GRPO)~ shao2024deepseekmath turns terminal task rewards into trajectory-level advantages by comparing rollouts collected for the same task. Each advantage is then applied across the rollout's action chunks. A terminal failure does not imply that every action contributed to failure. For example, a policy may drop an object, attempt to regrasp it, and exhaust its interaction budget (Figure~ fig:overview ). In a mixed-outcome group, the failed rollout's negative advantage penalizes both the error and the subsequent recovery attempts. This motivates the question: When to stop penalizing actions? Several methods already change which actions receive feedback, each at a different point in the pipeline. Temporal GRPO reconstructs stage-relative advantages but requires task-stage detection and rollout alignment~ zhou2026temporal . PCM allocates gradient computation through chunk sampling guided by phase-level success--failure divergence~ bagaria2026pcm . RedFlow's corrective targets require suitable successful matches in offline data~ yan2026redflow . In LLM reinforcement learning, negative-advantage updates are masked in -GRPO using importance-ratio triggers~ tian2026mugrpo . ESPO terminates rollouts early~ li2026espo , whereas PS-PPO samples update prefixes with importance weighting to preserve the reference gradient expectation~ hwang2026psppo . Here, failed-rollout suffixes are masked using visible errors and recovery cues after complete execution. Group advantages and original loss normalization are retained without additional correction weights for truncation. To identify a principled truncation boundary, we ask when future actions make no expected gradient contribution. At a fixed policy, the conditional success probability and the cumulative policy score are both martingales, and their increments carry that contribution. title: Retiming Robot Demonstrations with a Learned Speed Prior
summary: The pace of a robot demonstration is often determined by the teleoperator rather than by the task itself. As a result, the same motion can appear at widely different speeds across demonstrations, and policies trained on such data may inherit operator-specific timing along with task behavior. We propose to learn a speed prior directly from large-scale demonstration data. Given a task instruction, a motion path and the images along it, it predicts a distribution over execution speed along the path, from which a chosen quantile defines a consistent clock for retiming each demonstration. Existing methods derive the acceleration signal from the very data they accelerate, so each new task costs another fit, annotation, or pair of predefined rates. A single trained speed prior instead covers every task in a corpus. We fit a speed prior on both robot teleoperation data and handheld demonstrations in which a human arm, rather than a robot arm, moves the gripper, and use it to retime robot demonstrations to the handheld pace before fine-tuning a vision-language-action policy. For execution, we pair the policy with a real-time optimal-control layer that tracks predicted action chunks under robot constraints using the predicted pace. On 120 RoboLab tasks, policies fine-tuned on our learned clocks succeed more often and move with up to half the jerk compared with policies fine-tuned on the original demonstration timing and uniformly accelerated to the same speed. On a real robot, our policy stacks cups in 3.50s, 1.72$\times$ faster than the default policy's 6.02s while succeeding as often, in 29 of 30 trials. Videos and further material are available at https://mllab.snu.ac.kr/projects/learned_speed_prior.

Introduction The pace of robot demonstrations depends on both the collection setup and the operator. Moving a robot through a teleoperation interface is slower than moving a handheld gripper directly~ chi2024universal , and novice operators often hesitate or pause where experienced operators do not. Policies trained to imitate these demonstrations inherit the operators' pace along with the task behavior, often executing more slowly than necessary~ guo2025demospeedup,arachchige2025sail . Prior work speeds up such policies by retiming their demonstrations before or during training, or by accelerating their execution~ guo2025demospeedup,kim2026espada,sanchez2026volt,nam2025speedaug,jing2026tempovla,hu2026autospeed,arachchige2025sail,kim2026time . These methods shorten motion segments that require less precision, train the policy at a range of speeds, or execute the motion as fast as the robot's limits allow. They typically adjust the original demonstration timing based on task requirements, external speed commands, or robot limits. Few instead learn the pace from demonstrators who perform similar motions faster. We instead draw the pace from such demonstrators, for example those using a handheld gripper or experienced with the task, and give it to the demonstrations that the policy learns from. Their demonstrations need not follow the same paths, so we do not copy their timing but learn a speed prior, a model of how fast they move along a given path. Given the local shape of an end-effector path, the wrist-camera images along it and the task instruction, the prior predicts a distribution over the speed at which demonstrators traverse each part of the path. It is trained once on both kinds of demonstrations across all their tasks, with a label that marks the kind of each demonstration, so reading a path with the label of the faster demonstrators predicts how fast they would traverse it. A quantile of this distribution defines a clock that keeps the path of a demonstration but replaces its timing. We then fine-tune a policy on demonstrations retimed with the median clock and let it also predict tempo channels, the pace of higher quantiles, so that it can be sped up at deployment. The predicted pace reflects human motion and may therefore exceed the velocity, acceleration or torque limits of the robot. Joint PD control, commonly used to execute such policies, does not plan within these limits, so fast targets can cause tracking lag or safety reflexes~ khazatsky2024droid,intelligence2025openpi . Consecutive action chunks may also disagree at their boundaries, and each new chunk must accommodate the pace of the ongoing motion. We therefore introduce a controller that treats the predicted pace as an upper bound and executes each chunk as fast as the robot's limits permit, slowing down only where a limit becomes active. When a new chunk arrives, the controller smoothly connects it to the ongoing motion, preserving continuity in position, velocity, and acceleration while carrying the execution clock forward. We train the speed prior on teleoperated demonstrations from DROID and handheld demonstrations from FastUMI-100K, and use it to give DROID the handheld pace before fine-tuning the released DROID policy~ khazatsky2024droid,liu2025fastumi,intelligence2025pi05,intelligence2025openpi . On 120 tasks of the RoboLab simulation benchmark, this policy succeeds more often than a uniformly accelerated policy at the same speed-up, and at it does so with 52 less jerk~ yang2026robolab . Training only on fast demonstrations does not achieve this. A policy trained on the fastest DROID episodes alone, although their pace is that of all episodes, runs just faster than the policy trained on all of them. We observe the same on a real robot, where we adapt the prior to handheld demonstrations collected with a YUBI gripper and retime them to the pace of the shortest quarter of the episodes~ ohkawa2026yubi . Our policy stacks cups in s instead of s and succeeds in 29 of 30 trials, whereas a policy trained only on this quarter succeeds in 9 of 30 trials. On the same three-cup pyramid, SAIL reports s at a success rate of 0.40 for a diffusion policy trained on teleoperated demonstrations and accelerated by ~ arachchige2025sail , so our policy stacks them faster and succeeds more than twice as often. Finally, executing a human pace requires a controller that respects the robot's limits. With our controller in place of joint PD control, even the policy trained on the recorded timing folds the towel in 97 of trials instead of 13 . Related work Retiming demonstrations. A line of work changes the timing of demonstrations before policy training. Arc-length warping reparameterizes each trajectory by path length and leaves the speed to be chosen afterward~ braglia2025arc . ISR keeps a subset of the frames, spaced at roughly equal information, measured by velocity and acceleration~ yang2026improving . Others downsample the segments that do not require precision. DemoSpeedup finds them by the action entropy of a proxy policy trained on the task~ guo2025demospeedup . ESPADA labels a seed demonstration with vision-language and language models and propagates the labels to the other demonstrations of the task~ kim2026espada . VOLT prompts a vision-language model with examples from other tasks to label every demonstration~ sanchez2026volt . In these methods, the timing follows fixed criteria or is compressed by factors chosen by the user. Training policies at different speeds. Other methods retime demonstrations to a range of speeds during training and differ in how they choose the executed speed. SpeedAug trains the policy on demonstrations accelerated at random rates and then fine-tunes it with reinforcement learning in the task environment~ nam2025speedaug . TempoVLA conditions a vision-language-action policy on a speed command, which a vision-language model chooses at deployment~ jing2026tempovla . AutoSpeed learns a per-timestep speed by selecting, among candidates retimed at a discrete set of ratios, the one that best trades the policy's own prediction error against its prediction horizon~ hu2026autospeed . In all of these methods, the new timing is derived from the demonstration itself, the task at hand or an external command. In contrast, we draw the pace from other demonstrators who perform similar motions faster, and learn it as a speed prior shared across tasks. Executing policies faster. Learned policies usually send each predicted action as a position target to a PD controller, one action per time step of the demonstrations, which limits how much faster they can run~ khazatsky2024droid,intelligence2025openpi . SAIL predicts whether the current motion is critical, using labels obtained by clustering waypoints of the demonstrations, and scales the duration of each step by one of two factors~ arachchige2025sail . Realtime-VLA V2 retimes each chunk under velocity bounds with speeds from a model trained on the speed commands an operator gives during rollouts~ yang2026realtime . RACE retimes each chunk by time-optimal path parameterization, as fast as the velocity and torque limits of the robot allow~ pham2018new,kim2026time . Consecutive chunks are reconciled inside the policy or by the executor, as in VLA-RAIL, which joins them with quintic splines but scales their timing uniformly~ black2025real,black2025training,zhao2025vla . Other policies output controller parameters, such as the stiffness of an impedance controller~ martinmartin2019variable,kamijo2024learning,hou2025adaptive,kim2026compvla . Our policy likewise outputs its pace, and our controller follows this pace within the robot's dynamic limits and joins consecutive chunks without a jump in position, velocity or acceleration. title: SceneBloom: Agentic Indoor Environment Generation with Realistic and Diverse Layouts for Embodied Learning
summary: Training generalizable embodied agents requires realistic, varied, and simulation-ready indoor environments. Language-guided methods support semantic planning and object-level reasoning, but precise spatial grounding remains difficult. Visual generative models offer rich priors over plausible arrangements, yet their outputs require geometric reasoning to become physically valid 3D scenes. We introduce SceneBloom, an agentic framework that combines visual layout sampling with contract-guided 3D compilation. A hierarchical sampler uses diffusion priors to generate furniture arrangements within functional zones. A compiler then uses relations extracted from each proposal to guide geometric fitting and local pose correction. Across five room types, SceneBloom attains the highest visual quality and physical stability among the compared methods and is the only method with no detected mesh collisions and out-of-bounds objects. Its layouts are also closer to the distribution of real rooms than those of all compared baselines. Object navigation policies trained in these realistic scenes achieve a higher success rate in held-out real scans than those trained on an equal number of real training scans. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/scenebloom.

Overview of SceneBloom. SceneBloom compiles visual proposals of functional zones into a simulation-ready 3D scene, and resampling the same prompt yields different layouts. Its scenes are more physically plausible than those of prior generators and train a better object-navigation policy than an equal number of real scans. fig:teaser Introduction sec:intro Learning-based embodied agents benefit from training across varied environments. Prior work shows that procedurally generated environments support generalization across embodied tasks, and that language-guided scene generation can improve navigation in new scene types~ procthor2022,holodeck2024 . These findings motivate generators that provide diverse indoor layouts while retaining the spatial organization of real environments. Existing generators obtain layout structure from hand-crafted placement rules or learned distributions of 3D configurations~ procthor2022,diffuscene2024,physcene2024 , while language-guided and agentic systems combine flexible scene specification with spatial reasoning and iterative refinement~ holodeck2024,sceneweaver2025,sage2026,scenesmith2026 . Image diffusion models offer a complementary prior over how objects are arranged together. Recent methods exploit generated images and visual guidance to construct realistic 3D scenes~ architect2024,artiscene2025,scenethesis2025 . This suggests a division of responsibilities in which semantic planning establishes functional organization and visual sampling proposes detailed arrangements. The challenge is to carry those arrangements into geometrically valid 3D scenes. Visual plausibility alone is insufficient for this realization. Depth, scale, and pose errors from 3D lifting produce overlapping or misaligned furniture when the reconstructed objects are assembled, so geometric correction is necessary. Moving or rotating objects to resolve these conflicts, however, can break the relationships that made the sampled arrangement plausible, for example by turning a chair away from its desk. Our guiding insight is to separate the qualitative relationships to preserve from the numerical poses that must be repaired. We introduce SceneBloom, an agentic framework that implements this separation through two stages, hierarchical visual sampling and contract-guided 3D compilation. In the first stage, a vision--language planner divides the room into functional zones, using retrieved exemplar rooms as references, and specifies each zone's furniture inventory and approximate floor region. A diffusion model then samples a visual proposal of each zone's furniture arrangement, so that zoning supplies room-level structure while each proposal models one furniture group jointly. The diffusion model uses asset-specific adapters, each trained on renders of one catalog asset, so that the proposals depict the objects used for 3D construction. In the second stage, the proposals are lifted into 3D. Before any object is moved, a vision--language model extracts relation contracts from the proposal images, recording relationships such as facing, alignment, and proximity among the lifted objects. A hierarchical compiler then fits furniture within zones, assembles the zones into a room, and refines object poses to restore the contract relations. The contracts thus fix the relationships to preserve, while the compiler repairs only the numerical poses. Across five room types, SceneBloom scores highest on every visual-quality axis and on physical stability. It is also the only method with no detected mesh collisions and out-of-bounds objects. Its layouts more closely match real indoor layout distributions than all compared baselines on both Matterport3D~ matterport3d2017 and Scan2CAD~ avetisyan2019scan2cad . Ablations show that visual proposals outperform textual proposals on every metric, and that contract guidance further improves layout coherence and realism. For object navigation, a policy trained from scratch in our houses achieves higher success on held-out real scans than one trained on an equal number of real scans from the same dataset. Randomizing object placement within the same rooms removes most of this advantage, indicating that it arises from layout organization. Fine-tuning on our scenes also improves a pretrained policy, and controllable generation yields further gains by matching the difficulty of real homes. Our key contributions are: [leftmargin=1.5em] We introduce an agentic framework for generating diverse, realistic, simulation-ready indoor environments for embodied learning. It combines diffusion-based layout sampling with contract-guided 3D compilation to preserve functional organization while resolving geometric conflicts. We show that our scenes are both visually realistic and physically valid, and that their layouts align more closely with real rooms than those of all compared generators. We demonstrate that object navigation policies trained on our scenes transfer to real scanned environments better than those trained on real scans, and that controllable scene difficulty strengthens this transfer. Related Work sec:related 0.45 3D Indoor Scene Synthesis Procedural methods assemble indoor scenes under hand-crafted spatial rules~ procthor2022,infinigenindoors2024 , while autoregressive and diffusion models learn object configurations from annotated 3D scenes~ atiss2021,diffuscene2024,instructscene2024 . Physically guided variants further incorporate geometric constraints into layout sampling~ physcene2024,spread2026 . The arrangements of all these approaches remain bounded by the rules they encode or the 3D scenes they learn from. To draw on broader visual knowledge, image-guided methods generate scene proposals through whole-scene synthesis or progressive inpainting, then recover and refine 3D object placements~ artiscene2025,architect2024,scenethesis2025 . Although these methods bring rich visual priors into scene generation, image-level plausibility does not ensure compatibility with actual asset geometry, and correcting the resulting conflicts can disrupt the relationships that make the proposed layout functional. Our approach addresses both problems, since its proposals depict the actual assets to be placed and its compiler repairs their geometry under relation contracts extracted from the proposals. Language-Guided and Agentic Scene Generation Language-guided methods prompt an LLM to write an object inventory and spatial constraints, which a solver satisfies~ holodeck2024 . Agentic systems turn generation into a feedback loop, in which a planner selects generation and editing tools step by step~ sceneweaver2025,sage2026 or specialized agents divide scene design, critique, and workflow control~ scenesmith2026,scenemosaic2026 . Rendered views, geometric checks, and physics simulation guide each revision. Other work structures layout decisions through functional-zone graphs, semantic and physical decomposition, or compilable layout programs~ zonemaestro2026,stable2026,spatialgrammar2026 . Iterative refinement, however, repeats tool calls, rendering, and review, which slows generation~ sceneorchestra2026 , and errors in object orientation or in coordination across stages can leave arrangements functionally inconsistent~ sceneweaver2025,scenesmith2026 . Our framework uses agentic planning for functional zoning and diffusion sampling for furniture arrangement. Each zone's arrangement is thus sampled in one pass rather than revised object by object, and relation contracts keep it functional during 3D compilation. Synthetic Environments for Embodied Learning Synthetic environments provide controllable variation in the scenes and interactions for policy learning. Procedural and language-guided generators expand training coverage through alternative layouts, scene types, and object categories~ procthor2022,holodeck2024,divscene2024 . Studies of synthetic navigation datasets further show that scene realism matters alongside dataset size, motivating attention to object occurrence and spatial arrangement patterns~ hssd2024 . For manipulation, simulation frameworks pair varied environments and tasks with demonstrations~ robogen2023,robocasa2024,sage2026,robocasa3652026 . Real-to-sim approaches construct training scenes from observations, including families of alternative assets and configurations that retain relevant geometric and semantic affordances~ digitalcousins2024,simfoundry2026 . Together, these directions motivate training environments that combine variation with realistic spatial organization. SceneBloom provides both, and its generation settings can also adjust scene difficulty for policy learning. Contract-guided 3D compilation ( ) lifts these proposals into 3D, fits them into the room, and restores their functional relations before adding wall and surface objects. This division lets the visual prior supply plausible arrangements while compilation makes them physically valid. A vision--language model (VLM) plans the functional zones of the room, and a diffusion model then proposes the furniture arrangement of each zone as an image. Deciding which furniture a room needs and how the room divides into functional zones requires commonsense knowledge that a VLM has. title: SP-Guide: Enhancing Aerial Vision-Language Navigation with Spatial Priors
summary: Aerial vision-language navigation (AVLN) requires a UAV to reach a language-described target from partial egocentric observations while reasoning over large outdoor scenes. Existing approaches typically fuse view-centered RGB observations and globally anchored history maps as generic visual embeddings, leaving cross-modal spatial alignment to be learned from sparse navigation supervision. We present SP-Guide, a transformer- based goal-prediction framework that addresses this weakness of alignment through a Spatial Prior Cross-Modal Encoder, an Instruction Enhanced Decoder, and a Goal Convergence Filter for terminal target refinement. Experiments implemented on the CityNav benchmark show that SP-Guide improves success rate over the representative baselines, with the largest gains on unseen environments. These results indicate that physically grounded spatial priors provide an effective inductive bias for robust AVLN.

title: UniAction: Unified Action Conditioning for World Models
summary: Actions that condition world models are highly heterogeneous, and thus existing action-conditioned world models are typically built for individual action types, fragmenting already limited action-annotated data across separate models. We introduce UniAction, a unified action-conditioning framework that represents any action as a sparse set of action elements, each with a discrete semantic identity and a continuous spatiotemporal grounding coordinate. By mapping these coordinates directly into the pretrained video model's native positional space, UniAction allows heterogeneous actions to condition a shared world model within the same spatiotemporal structure. We further introduce cardinality-calibrated attention to address the bias from differing action representation granularities. We evaluate UniAction on four representative action forms: force, camera control, hand pose, and robot pose. UniAction outperforms conditioning alternatives in action following, and a single jointly trained model surpasses the action-specific experts, showing that heterogeneous action data benefit from unified model and joint training.

Project page: Introduction A world model predicts how the world evolves in response to actions~ parker2025genie,team2026advancing , and large-scale video generation models~ minimax2026h3, wan2025wan , which learn rich spatiotemporal dynamics from real-world videos, provide a natural foundation for building the world models~ brooks2024video . The actions that condition such world models, however, are highly heterogeneous. They range from global viewpoint changes~ parker2025genie,li2025hunyuan,tang2025hunyuan,sun2025worldplay,he2025matrix and physical forces applied to objects~ gillman2025force,gillman2026goal,physctrl2025,wang2026streaming to hand and robot motions~~ sudhakar2024controlling,xie2026generated,wang2025precise,zhu2025irasim , and differ greatly in their semantics and spatiotemporal structures. Given this heterogeneity, most existing action-conditioned world models are built for a single action type, with a conditioning mechanism designed for that type and training restricted to its data~ li2025hunyuan,sun2025worldplay,he2025matrix,gillman2025force,wang2026streaming,sudhakar2024controlling,zhu2025irasim . This practice is costly because action-annotated data is scarce: compared with large-scale generic video, it is limited in scale and concentrated in a narrow range of scenes and interaction patterns~ gillman2025force . Training separate models further fragments this data, and since each model learns how the world responds to only one type of action, knowledge of scene structure, object properties, and world dynamics that could be shared remains isolated across models~(Fig.~ fig:teaser , left). As the number of action types grows, such separate training scales poorly. To bring data from different actions into a single world model, we first need a conditioning representation that can accommodate their heterogeneous forms in a unified way. Existing generic mechanisms offer two natural choices. One renders actions into image or video conditions~ wang2025precise,wu2026oscar , providing direct spatial correspondence with the generated content, but not every action has a visual form that can be directly rendered. The other encodes different actions into conditioning tokens~ li2025multimodal,nvidia2025cosmos , which flexibly accommodates signals of different forms, but where and when an action takes effect in the generated video remains an implicit correspondence. These limitations lead us to reconsider what information heterogeneous actions actually need to convey to a world model. Our key observation is that, despite their heterogeneous raw forms, every action conveys two complementary pieces of information to the world model: what the action is, and where and when it takes effect. Based on this observation, we introduce , which represents each action as a sparse set of action elements. Each element describes its semantics with a discrete identity and its spatiotemporal grounding with a continuous coordinate. We place these coordinates directly in the pretrained video model's native positional geometry, allowing action and video to interact within a shared spatiotemporal structure while reusing the model's pretrained spatiotemporal modeling capabilities. Heterogeneous actions can thus condition a single model through the same mechanism without requiring a common raw representation or rendering into visual conditions. Since different actions may be represented by different numbers of elements, we further introduce cardinality-calibrated attention to prevent representation granularity from biasing conditioning strength. We instantiate on four representative action forms: force, camera control, hand pose, and robot pose. Under matched training settings, outperforms alternative conditioning mechanisms in both action following and visual quality. More importantly, a single jointly trained model consistently outperforms the corresponding action-specific experts across all four action forms~(Fig.~ fig:teaser , right), demonstrating the effectiveness of unified action conditioning and the benefit of jointly learning from heterogeneous action data. Our contributions are threefold: [nosep,leftmargin=*] We introduce , a unified action-conditioning framework that represents heterogeneous actions through action semantics and spatiotemporal grounding, placing action coordinates in the pretrained video model's native positional geometry so that all actions condition the model through the same mechanism. We introduce cardinality-calibrated attention to mitigate the bias caused by varying numbers of action tokens, reducing the influence of representation granularity on conditioning strength. Related Work Video World Models. Large-scale video generation models, such as Wan~ wan2025wan and MiniMax~ minimax2026h3 , learn visual structures and spatiotemporal dynamics through video pretraining, providing a generative foundation for predicting how the world evolves from current observations. Building on these powerful video models, a line of works~ parker2025genie,li2025hunyuan,he2025matrix,sun2025worldplay,gao2026infinite further introduce user interactions, enabling the models to continuously generate future observations of an environment under the given controls. These video world models typically define their action spaces and control interfaces for a specific environment; for example, the keyboard inputs and camera movement signals~ li2025hunyuan,he2025matrix . In contrast, builds on the same class of pretrained video models and allows actions from different environments with different structures to condition a single video world model through a shared interface. Action Conditioning in Video Models. Existing action-conditioned video models largely focus on specific action spaces. One line of work studies game commands, camera motion, and navigation controls~ li2025hunyuan,he2025matrix,sun2025worldplay,team2026advancing,gao2026infinite , while another models force-based physical interventions~ gillman2025force,gillman2026goal,physctrl2025,wang2026streaming with the environment. Other approaches condition video models on hand motion~ sudhakar2024controlling or robot manipulation trajectories~ zhu2025irasim . These methods typically use representations and conditioning mechanisms tailored to their respective action spaces. Recent work has begun to explore unifying related action spaces. Shared skeletal or kinematic representations connect human and robot motion~ wang2025precise,wu2026oscar , while the recent Cosmos 3~ agarwal2026cosmos represents controls across embodied systems through common physical variables. These approaches build on shared kinematic structures or common physical-control parameterizations. In contrast, accommodates heterogeneous actions with distinct structures and parameterizations through a shared formulation of action semantics and spatiotemporal grounding, enabling joint learning from diverse action-conditioned data within a single world model. Controllable Video Generation. Controllable video generation typically achieves unified control by converting external signals into shared conditioning representations compatible with the video model. Several approaches represent controls as visual conditions aligned with the generated video~ wang2023videocomposer,zhang2024controlvideo,jiang2025vace . However, this requires a suitable visual encoding for each control signal, which is less natural for abstract interventions such as forces. Alternatively, separate learned encoders can map different sensory inputs and actions into features that are fused and injected through a cross-attention mechanism~ li2025multimodal . These approaches accommodate heterogeneous inputs through either visual renderings or learned encoders for specific action formats. In contrast, directly represents actions following the same conditioning formulation at the representation level, without requiring a separate renderer or learned encoder for each action type. Action Semantics sec:action_semantics Action semantics describe the meaning represented by each action element. We define a shared discrete semantic vocabulary that distinguishes semantic identities both within and across action forms. A semantic codebook associates each identity with a -dimensional action token, where matches the feature dimension of the video tokens. For the -th action element, its semantic identity directly indexes the corresponding action token: . Each semantic identity is associated with an independently initialized action token, and the model learns its correspondence to scene evolution through joint action-conditioned training. Elements sharing the same identity reuse the same action token across different locations and times, while these spatiotemporal differences are modeled separately by the spatiotemporal grounding described in the next section. New semantic identities can be added directly to the same vocabulary, allowing the representation to naturally extend to new action forms. Spatiotemporal Grounding sec:spatiotemporal_grounding Spatiotemporal grounding specifies where and when an action element takes effect. Although heterogeneous actions may be defined in different coordinate and control spaces, their effects ultimately manifest in the spatiotemporal evolution of the generated video. We therefore use the video as a common spatiotemporal reference and represent the grounding of the -th action element with a continuous coordinate .
